Solute rejected at the solid-liquid interface (because the first solid to freeze is leaner in solute than the liquid it came from, per the phase diagram) diffuses away too slowly in the solid to erase the gradient, so each dendrite ends up with a composition profile: a solute-lean core, where it froze first, wrapped in progressively solute-richer shells outward. This layered composition within a single grain is called coring, and it is visible in polished, etched sections as concentric banding within individual dendrite arms.

sections.heading: Quantifying it: the Gulliver-Scheil relation
sections.body: The non-equilibrium solute redistribution during solidification was first worked out by G. H. Gulliver in 1913 and independently rederived by Erich Scheil in 1942, giving what is now usually called the Scheil equation (or Gulliver-Scheil equation). It assumes complete diffusion in the liquid (so the liquid stays uniform) but zero diffusion in the already-solidified material — the opposite extreme from the equilibrium lever rule — and predicts that the last liquid to freeze becomes progressively enriched in solute, following Cl = C0 fl^(k-1), where fl is the remaining liquid fraction and k is the partition coefficient. Because the last liquid to solidify sits at the dendrite arm boundaries and grain boundaries, that is exactly where solute (and any accompanying low-melting-point impurities) ends up concentrated, which is why segregation at grain boundaries so often creates a weak, corrosion-prone, or brittle interdendritic film.

sections.heading: From microsegregation to macrosegregation, and the fix
sections.body: Coring is microsegregation — a composition gradient within a single grain, on the scale of microns. Macrosegregation is the larger-scale version: composition variation across an entire ingot or casting, caused by bulk fluid flow of solute-enriched liquid (density-driven convection, or liquid squeezed out during shrinkage) redistributing solute over centimeters rather than microns before the casting fully solidifies. Related cast defects include shrinkage cavities and porosity — since most metals are denser as a solid than as a liquid, the last liquid to freeze in an isolated pocket cannot be fed by more liquid and leaves a void — and gas porosity, where dissolved gas (commonly hydrogen in aluminum or oxygen/nitrogen-scavenged gas in steel) has much lower solubility in the solid than the liquid and is rejected as bubbles during freezing. Because cored, segregated as-cast structures carry both composition gradients and weak interdendritic regions that hurt ductility and toughness, virtually no cast alloy destined for structural service is used in the as-cast state: a homogenization anneal, holding well below the solidus for hours, lets solid-state diffusion finally do what solidification was too fast to do, flattening the composition gradients and restoring a more uniform, single-phase microstructure before any further processing.

lessons.workedExample: A cast Cu-Ni bearing alloy is sectioned and examined under a microscope without etching for composition contrast; a student assumes the alloy is a uniform 70/30 blend throughout. Electron microprobe analysis across one dendrite arm instead shows nickel content starting near 45% at the dendrite core and falling to about 25% at the outer edge — classic coring, because nickel (the higher-melting-point, FCC-forming component) is preferentially incorporated into the first solid to freeze, per the Cu-Ni phase diagram's leaning liquidus/solidus. A 24-hour anneal at 1000°C, well below the ~1200-1300°C solidus for this composition, lets diffusion flatten that profile to a uniform ~30% Ni before the part is cold-worked and put into service.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots dendritic banding in a student's micrograph is testing whether the student understands it as a predictable consequence of non-equilibrium freezing rather than a flaw to explain away. A weak answer calls it 'impurities' or ignores it. A strong answer names coring, explains that fast cooling outruns solid-state diffusion so the first-formed solid is leaner in solute per the Scheil relation, and states the practical fix — homogenization annealing — rather than treating the defect as unfixable.

questions.prompt: What physically causes coring (a solute-lean core surrounded by solute-richer shells) within a single dendrite?

options.text: Contamination from the mold surface diffusing inward
Solid-state diffusion in the already-frozen material is too slow to keep up with the composition change predicted by the equilibrium phase diagram as freezing proceeds
The dendrite core is a different chemical element than the shell
Gravity pulls heavier atoms to the dendrite's outer edge

explanations.a: Coring is intrinsic to the solidification physics of the alloy itself, not contamination from the mold.
explanations.b: Correct — because the first solid to freeze is leaner in solute per the liquidus/solidus, and diffusion in the solid can't erase that gradient fast enough at typical cooling rates, each dendrite freezes with a built-in composition profile.
explanations.c: Coring is a concentration gradient of the same alloy's components, not a different element appearing.
explanations.d: Gravity-driven segregation exists at a much larger scale (macrosegregation) but is not the mechanism behind microscale coring within one dendrite.

questions.prompt: The Scheil equation assumes which combination of diffusion conditions?

options.text: Complete diffusion in both liquid and solid
No diffusion in either liquid or solid
Complete diffusion in the liquid, but zero diffusion in the solid
Complete diffusion in the solid, but zero diffusion in the liquid

explanations.a: That combination describes equilibrium (lever rule) freezing, not the Scheil case.
explanations.b: Zero diffusion in the liquid would prevent it from ever homogenizing, which is not what Scheil assumes.
explanations.c: Correct — Scheil (1942, building on Gulliver 1913) assumes the liquid stays uniform via fast diffusion/convection while the solid, once formed, is frozen in place with no further diffusion.
explanations.d: This is backwards; solid-state diffusion is the slow step, not the liquid.

questions.prompt: Why does interdendritic segregation often make the grain boundary region of a casting weaker or more corrosion-prone?

options.text: Grain boundaries are always weaker regardless of composition
The last liquid to solidify, which is enriched in solute and often low-melting impurities, ends up concentrated exactly at dendrite/grain boundaries
Grain boundaries contain no atoms at all
Segregation only affects the surface of the casting, never the interior boundaries

explanations.a: Grain boundary weakness in cast structures is specifically tied to what segregates there, not an inherent, composition-independent property.
explanations.b: Correct — per the Scheil-type redistribution, the last liquid to freeze is the most solute/impurity-enriched, and it solidifies precisely at the interdendritic and grain-boundary regions.
explanations.c: Grain boundaries are atomic interfaces, not voids; the issue is what composition ends up there.
explanations.d: Interdendritic segregation occurs throughout the casting's interior, not just at the surface.

questions.prompt: Match each cast defect to its cause.

right.text: Solid is denser than liquid, so the last isolated liquid pocket to freeze can't be fed and leaves a void
Dissolved gas has much lower solubility in solid than liquid and is rejected as bubbles during freezing
Bulk convective flow of solute-enriched liquid redistributes composition over centimeters, not microns

questions.explanation: Shrinkage cavities come from the solid-liquid density difference starving isolated pockets; gas porosity comes from gas solubility dropping sharply on freezing; macrosegregation comes from large-scale fluid flow, distinct from the micron-scale diffusion limits behind coring.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in addressing a cored as-cast structure, from the state right after casting to the state ready for service.

items.text: Casting freezes non-equilibrium, producing a cored dendritic structure with interdendritic segregation
Part is held at a high temperature well below the solidus for an extended time (homogenization anneal)
Solid-state diffusion flattens the composition gradient, yielding a more uniform microstructure

questions.explanation: Coring is created by fast non-equilibrium freezing, and it is corrected afterward by a homogenization anneal that gives slow solid-state diffusion enough time and temperature to finally erase the gradient.

lessons.label: Point Defects & Vacancies in Metals

sections.heading: No crystal is perfect, and that's thermodynamically required
sections.body: A vacancy is simply a missing atom — an empty lattice site where one should be. It costs energy to create (breaking bonds to remove an atom from the interior and place it, typically, at the surface or a grain boundary), so at absolute zero a perfect crystal has none. But above 0 K, thermodynamics forces some vacancies to exist even in a defect-free-grown crystal, because although creating a vacancy raises the internal energy, it also raises the configurational entropy — there are enormously many ways to distribute a handful of vacancies among billions of lattice sites — and above 0 K the system minimizes free energy (G = H - TS), not just energy. A small population of vacancies is therefore not a flaw to be engineered away; it is the equilibrium state of any real crystal at any real temperature. A self-interstitial, an atom squeezed into a gap between normal lattice sites rather than missing from one, is the less common companion defect, energetically far more costly in most metals because it distorts far more neighboring bonds than a vacancy does.

sections.heading: Why the population explodes with temperature
sections.body: Balancing the entropy gain against the enthalpy cost gives the equilibrium vacancy concentration Nv/N = exp(-Qv/kT), where Qv is the vacancy formation energy, k is Boltzmann's constant, and T is absolute temperature. This is an Arrhenius-type exponential, and the practical consequence is that vacancy concentration is essentially negligible at room temperature but rises steeply as the melting point is approached. Typical formation energies are around 0.7-0.8 eV for aluminum and roughly 0.9-1.3 eV for copper (values vary across formation-energy measurement techniques); plugging aluminum's value into the exponential near its melting point (933 K) gives an equilibrium vacancy fraction on the order of 10^-4 — meaning roughly one lattice site in ten thousand sits empty right before the metal melts, versus a fraction so small it is effectively zero at room temperature. Quenching a metal from near its melting point traps this high-temperature vacancy population in a supersaturated, non-equilibrium state at room temperature, because there isn't time for the excess vacancies to migrate out before the lattice 'freezes.'

sections.heading: Why this defect matters more than its tiny concentration suggests
sections.body: Vacancies matter because they are the vehicle for solid-state diffusion in most metals: an atom cannot move through a fully occupied lattice, but it can hop into an adjacent vacancy, and repeated hops let atoms migrate over macroscopic distances even though each individual jump only crosses one atomic spacing. This is why diffusion rates scale with vacancy concentration and inherit the same Arrhenius temperature dependence. Vacancies are also central to creep, the slow, time-dependent plastic deformation that shows up at high temperature and moderate stress in things like turbine blades, because vacancies enable dislocations to climb out of their glide planes and keep deforming the material even under sustained load below the ordinary yield stress. And they are essential to precipitation hardening: solute atoms diffusing together to form strengthening precipitates during an aging heat treatment can only do so as fast as vacancies let them move. Every later lesson on heat treatment and diffusion-controlled microstructure change is, underneath, a story about vacancy population and mobility.

lessons.workedExample: A metallurgy student quenches a piece of pure aluminum from 600°C into ice water, then ages it at room temperature and notices it hardens slightly over a few days even with no alloying addition intended to precipitate. The explanation: at 600°C (873 K), the equilibrium vacancy concentration was orders of magnitude higher than at 20°C, and the water quench cooled the metal far too fast for those excess vacancies to migrate to sinks (surfaces, grain boundaries) and disappear. The quenched-in vacancy supersaturation persists at room temperature and slowly annihilates over days, and because those same vacancies are what let any residual dissolved atoms diffuse, their presence measurably speeds up whatever slow atomic rearrangement is occurring — a live demonstration that vacancy concentration, not just alloy composition, controls diffusion-driven processes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does a vacancy concentration of one in ten thousand even matter?' to test whether a student sees vacancies as a mechanism rather than a curiosity. A weak answer describes a vacancy as just 'a missing atom' and stops there. A strong answer connects the exponential Nv/N = exp(-Qv/kT) relationship to a consequence the student actually used — diffusion rate, a quench-and-age result, or a creep failure — showing they understand vacancies as the rate-limiting carrier behind solid-state atomic motion, not an isolated fact.

questions.prompt: Why does a perfect crystal above 0 K always contain some equilibrium concentration of vacancies, even with no processing defects?

options.text: Vacancies are unavoidable manufacturing flaws that better casting technique could eliminate entirely
Creating vacancies raises entropy enough to lower the crystal's total free energy (G = H - TS) at any T > 0, even though it costs formation energy
Metal atoms spontaneously evaporate from the interior of the crystal
Vacancies are required to balance electrical charge in a metal

explanations.a: Equilibrium vacancies are thermodynamically required, not a processing flaw — no casting technique can reduce them below the equilibrium value at a given temperature.
explanations.b: Correct — the entropy gain from configurational disorder outweighs the enthalpy cost at any T above 0 K, so free energy minimization guarantees a nonzero equilibrium vacancy population.
explanations.c: Atoms don't literally evaporate from the interior; a vacancy forms by an atom relocating (typically to a surface or boundary), not disappearing.
explanations.d: Charge balance is a consideration in ionic ceramics, not in a metallic lattice where all sites hold the same element.

questions.prompt: The equilibrium vacancy concentration follows Nv/N = exp(-Qv/kT). What does this predict about vacancy concentration as temperature rises from room temperature toward the melting point?

options.text: It stays constant regardless of temperature
It decreases, since higher temperature stabilizes the perfect lattice
It rises exponentially, going from effectively negligible at room temperature to roughly one site in ten thousand for aluminum near its melting point
It rises linearly with temperature

explanations.a: The exponential form explicitly makes concentration temperature-dependent, not constant.
explanations.b: Higher temperature increases, not decreases, the entropy-driven vacancy population.
explanations.c: Correct — the Arrhenius-type exponential means vacancy concentration is essentially negligible near room temperature and climbs steeply near the melting point, reaching about 10^-4 for aluminum close to 933 K.
explanations.d: The dependence is exponential in 1/T, not linear in T, which is exactly why the rise is so steep near the melting point.

questions.prompt: Why does quenching a metal from near its melting point trap a supersaturated vacancy population at room temperature?

options.text: Quenching creates new vacancies that didn't exist at high temperature
The rapid cooling doesn't give the high-temperature equilibrium vacancy population enough time to migrate to sinks and disappear before the lattice is effectively locked in
Cold water chemically reacts with the metal surface to inject vacancies
Vacancy formation energy increases during quenching

explanations.a: The vacancies already existed at the high temperature; quenching doesn't create them, it preserves them.
explanations.b: Correct — vacancy annihilation at sinks (surfaces, boundaries) requires time and thermally activated migration, and a fast quench outruns that process, leaving a non-equilibrium excess frozen in.
explanations.c: This is a purely thermal/kinetic phenomenon, not a chemical reaction with the quenching medium.
explanations.d: Qv is a material property tied to bonding, not something that shifts during a quench.

questions.prompt: Match each phenomenon to the role vacancies play in enabling it.

right.text: Atoms move by hopping into adjacent empty lattice sites, letting them migrate over macroscopic distances
Vacancies let dislocations climb out of their glide plane, permitting continued slow deformation under sustained load
Solute atoms diffuse together to form strengthening particles, at a rate limited by vacancy-enabled atomic mobility

questions.explanation: All three phenomena are downstream of the same vacancy mechanism: diffusion is direct vacancy-mediated atomic hopping, creep depends on vacancy-enabled dislocation climb, and precipitation hardening depends on vacancy-mediated solute diffusion to form precipitates.

questions.prompt: Order these events in a quench-and-age experiment on pure aluminum, from first to last.

items.text: Aluminum is held at 600°C, reaching a relatively high equilibrium vacancy concentration
The metal is rapidly quenched into ice water, trapping the high-temperature vacancy population
At room temperature, the supersaturated vacancies slowly enable diffusion-driven changes over subsequent days

questions.explanation: The vacancy population is set at high temperature, frozen in by a fast quench that outruns vacancy annihilation, and only then does the trapped population drive slow room-temperature diffusion effects.

lessons.label: Diffusion: Fick's Laws & the Arrhenius Rate

sections.heading: Fick's first law: flux follows the gradient, not the concentration itself
sections.body: Adolf Fick's 1855 first law states that atomic flux J (atoms crossing a unit area per unit time) is proportional to the concentration gradient driving it: J = -D(dC/dx), where D is the diffusion coefficient and the negative sign reflects that net flow runs from high to low concentration, down the gradient. This is a steady-state law — it describes diffusion once the concentration profile has stopped changing with time, as in a thin membrane with a fixed concentration difference maintained on each side. Most real cases, though, are transient: a concentration profile that is still evolving, like carbon diffusing inward from a carburizing atmosphere at a steel part's surface. For that, Fick's second law, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²), governs how the concentration profile itself changes with time and position, and its solutions (often expressed with the error function for a semi-infinite solid with a fixed surface concentration) are what a metallurgist actually uses to design a carburizing or nitriding schedule.

sections.heading: Two mechanisms, and why the smaller atom has the easier path
sections.body: At the atomic level, diffusion in a solid happens by two mechanisms tied directly to the point defects. Vacancy diffusion moves substitutional atoms — same-size solute in the same lattice, or self-diffusion of the host atoms — one hop at a time into adjacent empty lattice sites, so its rate is capped by both the vacancy concentration and the energy to squeeze past neighboring atoms during the jump. Interstitial diffusion moves small solute atoms like carbon, nitrogen, or hydrogen through the gaps between host atoms without needing a vacancy at all, since interstitial sites are mostly empty to begin with. Because interstitial diffusion doesn't have to wait for a nearby vacancy and involves smaller, easier atomic movements, it is typically orders of magnitude faster than vacancy diffusion at a given temperature — carbon diffuses through iron dramatically faster than iron self-diffuses through iron, which is exactly why carburizing a steel surface in a matter of hours is practical while diffusing iron atoms themselves any comparable distance would take vastly longer.

sections.heading: The Arrhenius temperature dependence and the sqrt(Dt) rule that sets process time
sections.body: The diffusion coefficient itself is temperature-dependent, following an Arrhenius relationship D = D0 exp(-Qd/RT), where Qd is the activation energy for diffusion, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature — the same exponential form as the vacancy concentration, because vacancy-mediated diffusion inherits the vacancy population's own temperature sensitivity (and interstitial diffusion has its own, typically lower, Qd since it skips the vacancy-formation step). Practically, this means a modest temperature increase can multiply D many times over, which is why heat treaters push carburizing temperatures up (typically 850-950°C) rather than running the process longer at a lower temperature. The characteristic diffusion distance scales as x ≈ sqrt(Dt), a direct consequence of Fick's second law's solution form, and that square-root relationship has a blunt practical consequence: to double the case-hardened depth at a fixed temperature, the time must increase by a factor of four, not two, since x² ∝ Dt. A furnace operator who wants to double case depth without raising temperature is signing up for four times the furnace time, not twice.

lessons.workedExample: A shop carburizes a steel gear at 900°C for 4 hours and measures a case depth of 0.8 mm. The plant manager asks for 1.6 mm of case depth (double) using the same furnace temperature. Applying x ≈ sqrt(Dt) with D fixed by the unchanged temperature: doubling x requires quadrupling t, so the new cycle needs 16 hours, not 8. If instead the manager wants to hit 1.6 mm in the original 4 hours, the required D must be four times larger, which per the Arrhenius relation D = D0 exp(-Qd/RT) means raising the furnace temperature substantially — illustrating why real carburizing schedules are set by balancing temperature (which changes D exponentially) against time (which only changes penetration as its square root).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about diffusion timing to see if a student grasps the sqrt(Dt) scaling rather than assuming depth scales linearly with time. A weak answer says 'longer time means more diffusion' without a relationship. A strong answer states that penetration depth scales with the square root of time, so doubling depth costs four times the time at fixed temperature, and separately notes that raising temperature is a much more efficient lever because D depends exponentially on T through the Arrhenius relationship.

questions.prompt: Fick's first law, J = -D(dC/dx), is most appropriately applied to which situation?

options.text: A steady-state case where the concentration profile is no longer changing with time
A transient case where a carburizing profile is still evolving with time
Any diffusion situation, transient or steady-state, without distinction
Only diffusion of gases, never solids

explanations.a: Correct — Fick's first law describes flux under a fixed, unchanging concentration gradient, i.e., steady state.
explanations.b: A time-evolving profile like carburizing is the transient case, governed by Fick's second law instead.
explanations.c: The two laws are not interchangeable; the first law specifically assumes the profile has stopped changing.
explanations.d: Fick's laws apply broadly to diffusion in solids, liquids, and gases, not gases exclusively.

questions.prompt: Why is interstitial diffusion (e.g., carbon in iron) typically much faster than vacancy-mediated diffusion (e.g., iron self-diffusion) at a given temperature?

options.text: Interstitial atoms are magnetically attracted to move through the lattice
Interstitial diffusion doesn't need to wait for an adjacent vacancy, since interstitial sites are already mostly empty, and involves smaller, easier atomic movements
Vacancy diffusion only occurs above the melting point
Interstitial atoms are always larger than the atoms they diffuse past

explanations.a: Diffusion is driven by thermal activation and concentration gradients, not magnetism.
explanations.b: Correct — because interstitial sites are largely unoccupied to begin with, a small solute atom can hop from one to the next without needing a nearby vacancy, and the smaller displacement lowers the activation energy compared to squeezing a substitutional atom into a vacant lattice site.
explanations.c: Vacancy-mediated diffusion occurs in the solid state, well below the melting point; it's simply slower than interstitial diffusion, not restricted to above melting.
explanations.d: Interstitial solutes like carbon are specifically smaller than the host lattice atoms — that's precisely why they can occupy the gaps between them.

questions.prompt: A furnace operator wants to double the case-hardened depth of a carburized part while holding temperature (and thus D) fixed. Based on x ≈ sqrt(Dt), how much longer must the carburizing time be?

options.text: 2 times as long
4 times as long
The same time; only temperature affects depth
8 times as long

explanations.a: This would be true if depth scaled linearly with time, but the relationship is a square root, not linear.
explanations.b: Correct — since x ∝ sqrt(Dt), doubling x at fixed D requires t to increase by a factor of 2² = 4.
explanations.c: Time does affect depth at fixed temperature; it's just a square-root, not linear, relationship.
explanations.d: 8x would follow a cube relationship, which doesn't match the sqrt(Dt) form of Fick's second law's solution.

questions.prompt: Match each diffusion term to what it represents.

right.text: A pre-exponential (temperature-independent) constant specific to the diffusing species and lattice
The activation energy for the atomic jump, which sets how strongly D depends on temperature
The concentration gradient that drives the direction and magnitude of atomic flux

questions.explanation: D0 is the pre-exponential constant, Qd is the activation energy controlling the Arrhenius temperature sensitivity of D, and dC/dx is the driving force in Fick's first law.

questions.prompt: Order these carburizing case depths from SMALLEST to LARGEST required diffusion time at a fixed temperature, given x ∝ sqrt(Dt).

items.text: Case depth x (baseline time t)
Case depth 2x (requires 4t)
Case depth 3x (requires 9t)

questions.explanation: Because x scales with the square root of time at fixed D, required time scales with the square of the depth ratio: doubling depth needs 4x the time, and tripling depth needs 9x the time.

lessons.label: Dislocations & Slip: How Metals Deform Plastically

sections.heading: Two flavors of line defect, and the vector that unifies them
sections.body: A dislocation is a line defect — a one-dimensional disruption in the otherwise regular stacking of a crystal lattice. An edge dislocation is best pictured as an extra half-plane of atoms wedged into the lattice, terminating partway through the crystal; the atoms just below that termination line are compressed and pushed apart, creating a localized strain field. A screw dislocation instead looks like the lattice has been sheared into a spiral ramp around the dislocation line, with no extra half-plane at all. Both are fully characterized by the Burgers vector b, defined by tracing a closed loop (a Burgers circuit) around the dislocation in the real, defected crystal and noting the vector needed to close the same loop in a perfect reference lattice — the resulting mismatch is b. For an edge dislocation b is perpendicular to the dislocation line; for a screw dislocation b is parallel to it; most real dislocations are mixed, some combination of the two, and b stays fixed along the whole dislocation regardless of how its character changes.

sections.heading: Slip systems and why crystal structure dictates ductility
sections.body: Plastic deformation in metals happens overwhelmingly by slip: a dislocation glides along a specific crystallographic plane, in a specific crystallographic direction, and the combination of a slip plane and a slip direction within it is a slip system. Dislocations preferentially glide on the most densely packed planes, in the most densely packed directions, because that minimizes the Burgers vector's magnitude and the energy of the dislocation core. Face-centered cubic metals — copper, aluminum, nickel, austenitic stainless steel — slip on the {111} planes in <110> directions, giving 12 slip systems, of which 5 are independent, meeting the von Mises minimum — and that abundance of easy slip paths is the direct structural reason FCC metals are so ductile, capable of large plastic strains before fracture. Hexagonal close-packed metals like magnesium, zinc, and titanium have far fewer easily activated slip systems at room temperature — typically just the basal plane, offering only a few independent systems well short of the five independent systems the von Mises criterion says a polycrystal needs for arbitrary shape change — which is why HCP metals tend to be comparatively brittle at room temperature and often need elevated temperature or additional deformation mechanisms like twinning to accommodate large strains.

sections.heading: Schmid's law and why real metals are far weaker than theory predicts
sections.body: Erich Schmid's 1924 relation formalizes how much of an applied stress resolves onto a slip plane in the slip direction: the resolved shear stress τ = σ cos(φ) cos(λ), where σ is the applied uniaxial stress, φ is the angle between the stress axis and the slip plane normal, and λ is the angle between the stress axis and the slip direction. Slip begins once τ reaches a material- and system-specific threshold called the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS); the grain orientation with the largest cos(φ)cos(λ) product (the Schmid factor, maximum 0.5) yields first. This single-dislocation-at-a-time glide mechanism is also the resolution to a decades-old puzzle: the theoretical shear strength of a defect-free crystal, estimated from the interatomic bonding forces (roughly G/2π by Frenkel's 1926 estimate, where G is the shear modulus), predicts strengths thousands of times higher than what real metals actually exhibit. Real metals typically yield at only about 1/1000 (order of magnitude) of that theoretical strength — a discrepancy first reconciled once dislocations were proposed independently by Geoffrey Ingram Taylor, Michael Polanyi, and Egon Orowan in 1934.

lessons.workedExample: A single crystal of copper is pulled in tension along an axis where the {111}<110> slip plane normal sits 45° from the tensile axis (φ=45°) and the slip direction sits 45° from the tensile axis as well (λ=45°) — the orientation that maximizes the Schmid factor, cos(45°)cos(45°) = 0.5. If copper's CRSS is roughly 1 MPa (a typical order-of-magnitude value for well-annealed, low-dislocation-density copper), the applied stress needed to initiate slip is σ = τ/(cos φ cos λ) = 1 MPa / 0.5 = 2 MPa. A second crystal of the same copper, cut so its slip system sits at φ=80°, λ=80° (Schmid factor cos(80°)cos(80°) ≈ 0.03), needs roughly 33 MPa to reach the same 1 MPa resolved shear stress — showing that yield stress in a single crystal is not a fixed material constant but depends heavily on crystallographic orientation relative to the loading axis.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a strength or ductility claim wants to see whether a student can explain deformation mechanistically rather than citing a datasheet number. A weak answer says a metal is 'strong' or 'ductile' with no mechanism. A strong answer names slip and dislocation glide as the deformation mechanism, ties FCC's 12 slip systems (versus HCP's few) to an observed ductility difference, and can state that real yield strengths sit orders of magnitude below the theoretical shear strength precisely because dislocations glide one row of bonds at a time instead of requiring a whole plane to shear at once.

questions.prompt: What geometric feature distinguishes an edge dislocation from a screw dislocation?

options.text: An edge dislocation involves an extra half-plane of atoms terminating in the crystal; a screw dislocation shears the lattice into a spiral ramp with no extra half-plane
An edge dislocation only occurs in FCC metals; a screw dislocation only occurs in HCP metals
An edge dislocation has no Burgers vector; a screw dislocation does
Edge and screw dislocations are the same defect described in different units

explanations.a: Correct — the extra half-plane defines the edge dislocation, while the spiral-ramp shear with no extra plane defines the screw dislocation.
explanations.b: Both dislocation types can occur in any crystal structure; the FCC/HCP distinction is about which slip systems are available, not which dislocation type exists.
explanations.c: Every dislocation, edge or screw, has a well-defined Burgers vector; that's what makes it a dislocation rather than some other defect.
explanations.d: They are geometrically distinct defects, distinguished by the relationship between the Burgers vector and the dislocation line direction.

questions.prompt: Why are FCC metals like copper and aluminum generally more ductile than HCP metals like magnesium at room temperature?

options.text: FCC metals have 12 {111}<110> slip systems (5 independent), while HCP metals typically have only a few easily activated slip systems at room temperature
FCC metals contain no dislocations, so they deform without resistance
FCC metals have a lower melting point, which always increases ductility
HCP metals have a larger Burgers vector, which prevents any slip

explanations.a: Correct — 12 slip systems (5 of them independent, meeting the von Mises minimum) give dislocations many more paths to accommodate an arbitrary shape change, which is the structural basis for FCC's characteristic ductility.
explanations.b: Dislocations are present and essential in FCC metals too; ductility comes from having many slip systems for them to glide on, not from their absence.
explanations.c: Melting point is not the controlling factor here; slip system count tied to crystal structure is.
explanations.d: HCP metals do slip, just on fewer independent systems; a larger Burgers vector alone doesn't prevent slip.

questions.prompt: Per Schmid's law, τ = σ cos(φ) cos(λ), what is the maximum possible Schmid factor, and what does it mean physically?

options.text: 1.0, reached when the slip plane and slip direction are both parallel to the applied stress axis
0.5, reached when both φ and λ equal 45°, the orientation most favorable for resolving applied stress onto the slip system
0, because resolved shear stress is always smaller than applied stress
2.0, because cos(φ) and cos(λ) can each exceed 1

explanations.a: A slip plane oriented parallel to the stress axis (φ=90° from the axis, i.e. the normal perpendicular) would give zero resolved shear stress on that plane, not the maximum.
explanations.b: Correct — the product cos(φ)cos(λ) is maximized at 0.5 when φ=λ=45°, which is why that orientation yields first under a given applied stress.
explanations.c: Resolved shear stress is smaller than applied stress except at the maximum Schmid factor, but it is never exactly zero for all orientations — that's a mischaracterization of the geometry.
explanations.d: Cosine values are bounded between -1 and 1, so the product cannot exceed 1, let alone 2.

questions.prompt: Real metals yield at roughly what fraction of their theoretical shear strength (estimated from interatomic bonding, ~G/2π), and why?

options.text: About 1/1000, because dislocation glide lets slip occur one row of bonds at a time instead of requiring an entire atomic plane to shear simultaneously
About 1/2, because only half the atoms in a plane bond at once
Essentially the full theoretical value, because real metals have no defects
About 1/1000, because metals are mostly empty space between atoms

explanations.a: Correct — this is the classic resolution (Taylor, Polanyi, and Orowan, 1934) to the strength discrepancy: dislocations let a crystal deform by breaking and reforming one row of bonds at a time, requiring far less stress than shearing a whole plane at once.
explanations.b: This isn't the actual ratio, and 'half the atoms bonding' isn't the mechanism responsible for the strength gap.
explanations.c: Real metals are full of dislocations, which is exactly why their strength falls so far below the defect-free theoretical estimate.
explanations.d: The correct fraction is right, but 'empty space between atoms' is not the actual mechanism — dislocation glide is.

questions.prompt: Match each person/concept to what they are credited with.

right.text: Formalized the resolved shear stress relation τ = σ cos(φ) cos(λ)
Independently proposed the dislocation as the carrier of plastic slip
Estimated the theoretical shear strength of a defect-free crystal from interatomic bonding

questions.explanation: Schmid formalized resolved shear stress and CRSS; Taylor, Polanyi, and Orowan independently proposed dislocations in 1934 to explain why real yield strength is so much lower than theory; Frenkel's earlier estimate of theoretical shear strength from bonding forces set up the puzzle dislocations solved.

units.label: Binary Phase Diagrams & the Lever Rule

lessons.label: Reading a Phase Diagram: Components, Phases & the Gibbs Rule

sections.heading: Two axes, one map of equilibrium
sections.body: A binary phase diagram plots temperature against composition (usually weight percent of one component) and marks off the regions where each combination is stable at equilibrium. The number of components, C, is the number of chemically independent species — copper and nickel give C=2 regardless of how many phases those two elements form. A phase is a physically distinct, chemically uniform region: liquid, a solid solution, or a compound each count separately even if they share elements. The diagram's boundary lines matter as much as the fields between them. The liquidus is the line above which everything is liquid; the solidus is the line below which everything is solid. Between them lies a two-phase field where liquid and solid coexist — this band is the region every casting and welding process must pass through, and its width controls how much segregation and porosity a real part develops.

sections.heading: The Gibbs phase rule constrains the map
sections.body: Josiah Willard Gibbs derived the general phase rule, F = C - P + 2, in a series of papers published by the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences between 1875 and 1878, where F is the number of degrees of freedom (independent variables like temperature or composition you can change without changing which phases are present), C is components, and P is phases. Materials engineers work at fixed atmospheric pressure, so one degree of freedom is already used up, giving the condensed form F = C - P + 1. In a single-phase field of a binary system (C=2, P=1), F=2: you can vary both temperature and composition freely. In a two-phase field (P=2), F=1: fix the temperature and the compositions of both phases are pinned by the diagram — you cannot choose them. At an invariant reaction (P=3, covered later for eutectics), F=0: temperature and both compositions are fixed points, not ranges.

sections.heading: Equilibrium maps versus real cooling
sections.body: Every line on a standard phase diagram assumes infinitely slow cooling, giving atoms enough time to diffuse and each phase to reach its equilibrium composition throughout. Real furnace or mold cooling rates are far faster, so actual microstructures often show compositional gradients and phase fractions that the equilibrium diagram alone does not predict — a gap explored fully once non-equilibrium (Scheil-type) cooling is introduced later in this unit. For now, treat the diagram as the destination a slowly cooled alloy would reach, not a literal recipe for what any particular furnace run produces.

lessons.workedExample: For a Cu-Ni alloy at 35 wt% Ni and 1250°C, first locate that point on the Cu-Ni diagram: it falls inside the two-phase alpha-plus-liquid field, between the liquidus and solidus (the 1250°C tie line for this composition crosses the liquidus at about 32 wt% Ni and the solidus at about 43 wt% Ni). Applying the phase rule with C=2, P=2 gives F=1 — temperature is the one free variable, so once 1250°C is fixed, the compositions of the solid and liquid are pinned wherever the horizontal isotherm at 1250°C crosses the solidus and liquidus. A student who instead reports 'F=2' has forgotten to subtract for the second phase, and would wrongly expect to also choose the liquid's composition independently of temperature — which the diagram does not allow.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a phase-diagram poster will ask 'how many phases can coexist at that point, and how do you know?' because it tests whether the student is reading the diagram as a real equilibrium tool rather than a decorative chart. A weak answer names a temperature and composition but cannot say how many phases are present or why. A strong answer states the phase count from the field the point sits in, and can connect that to degrees of freedom — showing they understand the diagram encodes a physical constraint, not just a color-coded region.

questions.prompt: Using the condensed Gibbs phase rule F = C - P + 1 for a binary system (C=2) at fixed pressure, what is F inside a two-phase field?

explanations.a: F=2 applies to a single-phase field (P=1), where both temperature and composition can vary freely.
explanations.b: Correct — with C=2 and P=2, F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1: once temperature is fixed, the phase compositions are pinned by the liquidus and solidus.
explanations.c: F=0 applies to an invariant three-phase reaction like a eutectic point, not an ordinary two-phase field.
explanations.d: F cannot exceed C=2 for the condensed rule (reached only at P=1), so F=3 would require P=0 phases, which never happens.

questions.prompt: Why does materials engineering use F = C - P + 1 instead of Gibbs's original F = C - P + 2?

options.text: Because solid alloys never have more than one phase
Because pressure is held fixed at 1 atm, removing one degree of freedom
Because temperature is not considered a variable in metallurgy
Because composition is not a true degree of freedom

explanations.a: Solid alloys routinely show multiple phases, such as eutectic microstructures with two solids.
explanations.b: Correct — condensed-system phase diagrams are built at constant atmospheric pressure, so one of Gibbs's original variables is already fixed, dropping the +2 to +1.
explanations.c: Temperature is one of the two axes of every phase diagram and is very much a variable.
explanations.d: Composition is exactly the second axis and a genuine degree of freedom in single-phase fields.

questions.prompt: Match each phase-diagram feature to its definition.

right.text: Line above which the alloy is entirely liquid
Line below which the alloy is entirely solid
Region between liquidus and solidus where liquid and solid coexist

questions.explanation: The liquidus caps the fully liquid region from above, the solidus caps the fully solid region from below, and every composition cooling between them passes through a two-phase liquid-plus-solid field.

questions.prompt: Order these from fewest to most degrees of freedom (F) in a binary condensed system.

items.text: Invariant three-phase reaction point
Two-phase field
Single-phase field

questions.explanation: F = C - P + 1 with C=2 gives F=0 at P=3 (invariant point), F=1 at P=2 (two-phase field), and F=2 at P=1 (single-phase field) — freedom rises as the phase count falls.

lessons.label: Isomorphous Systems & the Tie Line

sections.heading: Complete solubility: the Cu-Ni case
sections.body: An isomorphous system is one where the two components are completely soluble in each other in both the liquid and solid states, so a single solid-solution phase (conventionally labeled alpha) exists across the entire composition range below the solidus. Copper and nickel are the textbook example: both crystallize as face-centered cubic metals, their atomic radii differ by only about 2.5 percent, and their electronegativities and valences are close — exactly the conditions William Hume-Rothery laid out in 1934 for extensive substitutional solid solubility. The Cu-Ni diagram has no eutectic, no compound, and no invariant reaction; it is just a liquidus running from pure copper's melting point (1085°C) up to pure nickel's (1453°C), a solidus tracking beneath it, and the alpha solid-solution field below that. Because there is only one solid phase, every alloy in the system solidifies gradually across a temperature range rather than at one sharp point.

sections.heading: The tie line reads off two compositions from one point
sections.body: Inside the two-phase alpha-plus-liquid field, a single point tells you only the overall (average) composition and temperature — it does not by itself tell you what the liquid or the solid actually contains. To extract those, draw a horizontal isotherm across the two-phase field at that temperature: this is the tie line. Where it intersects the liquidus gives the composition of the liquid in equilibrium at that temperature; where it intersects the solidus gives the composition of the solid. Because nickel raises the melting point, the solidus composition is always richer in nickel than the liquidus composition at any given temperature inside the loop — the solid that forms first is enriched in the higher-melting component.

sections.heading: Compositions migrate as the alloy cools
sections.body: Follow a fixed overall composition, say 35 wt% Ni, as it cools from the liquid. At the temperature where the vertical composition line first touches the liquidus, an infinitesimal amount of solid nucleates, and its composition (read from the solidus at that temperature) is far richer in nickel than the liquid. As cooling continues, the tie line sweeps downward: the liquid composition slides along the liquidus toward lower nickel content, and the solid composition slides along the solidus, also toward lower nickel content, converging until the vertical line meets the solidus and the last liquid disappears at the overall 35 wt% Ni composition. This continuous shift is why isomorphous alloys need slow cooling and diffusion to avoid the coring behavior covered later in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A Cu-Ni alloy at the overall composition 35 wt% Ni is held at 1250°C, inside the two-phase field. Drawing the 1250°C tie line, it crosses the liquidus at about 32 wt% Ni and the solidus at about 43 wt% Ni. So at that instant the liquid contains 32% Ni and the coexisting solid contains 43% Ni — neither equals the alloy's nominal 35% Ni, which is only the system-wide average of the two. A common mistake is to read the single point's x-coordinate (35%) as if it were the composition of one of the phases; the tie line's two endpoints, not the point itself, give the real phase compositions.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe tie-line reading because it exposes whether a student can extract quantitative phase information from a diagram rather than just naming regions. A weak presenter says 'the alloy is 35% nickel' as if that describes the solid or the liquid. A strong presenter draws or describes the horizontal isotherm, reports two different endpoint compositions, and explains why the solid is richer in the higher-melting element — showing they grasp that a two-phase point is an average of two distinct materials, not one uniform one.

questions.prompt: In the Cu-Ni system, why does the solid phase in equilibrium with liquid always contain more nickel than the liquid at the same temperature?

options.text: Because nickel atoms are smaller and pack into the solid preferentially
Because nickel has the higher melting point, so the solidifying phase is enriched in it
Because copper evaporates preferentially from the liquid
There is no such rule; it depends on which alloy is being cooled

explanations.a: Atomic size difference (about 2.5%) is why the system is isomorphous at all, but it is not what sets which phase is nickel-rich.
explanations.b: Correct — the higher-melting component (Ni, 1453°C vs Cu's 1085°C) is thermodynamically favored in the solid at any given temperature within the loop, so the solidus sits at higher Ni content than the liquidus.
explanations.c: Evaporation is not a mechanism the equilibrium phase diagram accounts for.
explanations.d: The enrichment direction is a consistent feature of the Cu-Ni loop at every temperature within the two-phase field.

questions.prompt: A point sits inside the alpha-plus-liquid field at 35 wt% Ni overall. What does the tie line's liquidus-side endpoint represent?

options.text: The average composition of the whole alloy
The composition of the solid phase present
The composition of the liquid phase present
The composition the alloy will have after full solidification

explanations.a: The 35% figure is the overall average; the tie line endpoints give the two individual phase compositions, which differ from it.
explanations.b: The solidus-side endpoint, not the liquidus-side endpoint, gives the solid's composition.
explanations.c: Correct — where the isotherm crosses the liquidus is, by definition, the composition of the liquid phase at that temperature.
explanations.d: After full solidification the alloy is single-phase alpha at the original 35% Ni; that endpoint describes an intermediate liquid, not the final state.

questions.prompt: Match each Hume-Rothery-style condition to why it favors complete solid solubility in Cu-Ni.

right.text: Allows one element's lattice to host the other without a structural transition
Minimizes lattice strain from substituting one atom for another
Avoids strong compound-forming tendencies between unlike atoms

questions.explanation: Hume-Rothery's 1934 conditions for extensive substitutional solubility are matching crystal structure, comparable atomic size, and similar chemical character — all three hold for Cu and Ni, which is why the system is isomorphous with no compounds or eutectic.

questions.prompt: Order these events as a 35 wt% Ni Cu-Ni alloy cools slowly from a fully liquid state to fully solid.

items.text: Alloy is entirely liquid, above the liquidus
First solid nucleates at the liquidus temperature, rich in Ni
Tie line sweeps down; liquid and solid compositions both drift toward lower Ni
Last liquid vanishes at the solidus; alloy is single-phase alpha at 35% Ni

questions.explanation: Cooling starts fully liquid, first solid appears at the liquidus (enriched in the higher-melting Ni), both phase compositions shift along their respective boundaries as temperature drops, and solidification completes at the solidus where the last liquid disappears.

lessons.label: The Lever Rule: Calculating Phase Amounts

sections.heading: A mass balance in disguise
sections.body: The tie line tells you what each phase's composition is, but not how much of each phase is present — that comes from the lever rule, which is nothing more than conservation of mass written along the tie line. Suppose the overall alloy composition is C0, and the tie line at a given temperature runs from a solid-phase composition C_alpha to a liquid-phase composition C_L, with C0 lying between the two endpoint compositions (in Cu-Ni, C_L < C0 < C_alpha, since the solid is enriched in the higher-melting component). If W_alpha and W_L are the weight fractions of solid and liquid, mass balance on the solute requires W_alpha + W_L = 1 and W_alpha*C_alpha + W_L*C_L = C0. Substituting W_alpha = 1 - W_L and solving gives W_L = (C0 - C_alpha) / (C_L - C_alpha) and W_alpha = (C_L - C0) / (C_L - C_alpha). The name comes from the mechanical analogy: treat the tie line as a rigid lever balanced at C0, with the phase amounts acting like weights at the two ends — the classic 'weight times arm' balance of a lever.

sections.heading: The far-arm rule, and where students go wrong
sections.body: The formulas above encode a rule that is easy to state backward: the weight fraction of a phase equals the length of the tie-line segment on the OPPOSITE side of C0, divided by the total tie-line length. W_L uses (C0 - C_alpha), the segment measured from the solid end up to C0 — not the segment from C0 to the liquid end. This is the single most common error in applying the lever rule: taking the near arm (the segment adjacent to the phase you're solving for) instead of the far arm (the segment on the other side of C0, away from that phase). A fast sanity check catches the mistake every time: if C0 sits very close to C_alpha, physically almost all the material must be solid, so W_alpha should come out close to 1 — and only the far-arm formula, (C_L - C0)/(C_L - C_alpha), gives a value near 1 in that limit, since C_L - C0 is then nearly the full tie-line length.

sections.heading: Weight fraction versus atomic or volume fraction
sections.body: Phase diagrams are almost always plotted in weight percent, so the lever rule as derived directly yields weight fractions of each phase, not volume fractions. Converting to volume fraction — needed, for instance, to predict how a two-phase microstructure will look under a microscope — requires the densities of each phase, since a given mass of a light phase occupies more volume than the same mass of a dense one. This distinction rarely appears in an introductory lever-rule problem, but it is worth flagging explicitly, because a science-fair judge who has done metallography will ask which fraction was actually measured on a micrograph.

lessons.workedExample: A Cu-Ni alloy at 35 wt% Ni sits at a temperature where the tie line gives C_alpha = 43 wt% Ni (solid) and C_L = 32 wt% Ni (liquid). Applying the far-arm formula for the liquid fraction: W_L = (C0 - C_alpha)/(C_L - C_alpha) = (35 - 43)/(32 - 43) = (-8)/(-11) ≈ 0.73, so about 73% liquid and 27% solid at that instant. Note C0=35 is closer to C_L=32 than to C_alpha=43, so most of the material should be liquid — and 73% liquid matches that intuition, confirming the far-arm assignment was done correctly rather than accidentally inverted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands phase diagrams will often hand a student a specific temperature and composition and ask them to compute the phase fractions on the spot, because the lever rule is where 'I can describe the diagram' and 'I can extract a number from it' diverge. A weak answer plugs numbers into a memorized formula without checking whether the result makes physical sense. A strong answer states which arm is the far arm before calculating, and sanity-checks the result against where C0 sits relative to the two endpoints — catching a near/far mix-up before it reaches the poster.

questions.prompt: For a tie line with C_alpha = 43 wt% Ni (solid) and C_L = 32 wt% Ni (liquid), overall composition C0 = 35 wt% Ni, which expression correctly gives the weight fraction of liquid?

options.text: (C_L - C_alpha) / (C0 - C_alpha)
(C0 - C_alpha) / (C_L - C_alpha)
(C_L - C0) / (C_L - C_alpha)
(C0 - C_L) / (C0 - C_alpha)

explanations.a: This inverts the ratio and does not stay bounded between 0 and 1 in general; it is not the lever rule.
explanations.b: Correct — the weight fraction of liquid uses the far arm, the segment from the solid-side endpoint C_alpha to C0, divided by the full tie-line length.
explanations.c: This is the far-arm formula for the SOLID fraction, not the liquid fraction — a classic label swap.
explanations.d: This mixes numerator and denominator terms in a way that does not reduce to a valid mass balance.

questions.prompt: An overall composition C0 sits very close to C_alpha (the solid-phase composition) on the tie line. Physically, what should the calculated weight fraction of solid, W_alpha, be close to?

options.text: It cannot be determined without densities

explanations.a: A near-zero solid fraction would mean the alloy is almost all liquid, which contradicts C0 sitting near the solid composition.
explanations.b: An even 50/50 split would only occur if C0 were roughly midway between C_alpha and C_L, not close to C_alpha.
explanations.c: Correct — if the overall composition is nearly identical to the solid's composition, nearly all the mass must be solid, so W_alpha approaches 1. This is the sanity check that catches a near/far arm mix-up.
explanations.d: The lever rule gives weight fractions directly from compositions alone; densities are only needed to convert to volume fractions, not weight fractions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to correctly apply the lever rule at a chosen temperature.

items.text: Draw the horizontal tie line at that temperature
Read off the two phase compositions at the tie line's endpoints
Identify the far arm (opposite side of C0 from the phase of interest)
Divide the far arm's length by the total tie-line length

questions.explanation: You must first locate the tie line and its endpoint compositions before any arm can be measured, then correctly identify which arm is opposite the phase you're solving for, and only then compute the ratio.

lessons.label: Eutectic Systems & Microstructure

sections.heading: One liquid, two solids, one temperature
sections.body: A eutectic system forms when the two components have limited solid solubility in each other, so instead of one continuous solid-solution field like Cu-Ni, the diagram has two separate solid solutions (alpha, rich in one component, and beta, rich in the other) separated by a two-phase alpha-plus-beta field. The liquidus lines from each pure-metal melting point slope downward and meet at a single low point called the eutectic point, where the invariant reaction L → alpha + beta occurs entirely at one fixed temperature and one fixed liquid composition. By the phase rule, F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0 at that point: three phases coexist with zero degrees of freedom, so the reaction proceeds isothermally, not over a range, unlike ordinary solidification.

sections.heading: Pb-Sn solder and Al-Si castings
sections.body: The lead-tin system is the textbook eutectic: its eutectic point sits at 61.9 wt% Sn and 183°C, well below either pure metal's melting point (Pb 327°C, Sn 232°C) — exactly the depressed-melting-point behavior that made Sn-Pb solder standard in electronics assembly for decades. At the exact eutectic composition (61.9 wt% Sn, close to the common 63/37 solder), the alloy solidifies isothermally with no mushy pasty range; the more common 60/40 solder is slightly off-eutectic, with a solidus around 183°C but a liquidus a few degrees higher, so it freezes through a narrow pasty range that eutectic 63/37 avoids — one reason eutectic solder was often favored for wave and hand soldering despite 60/40's widespread historical use. Lead-based solder was phased out of most consumer electronics after the EU's RoHS directive took effect in 2006, pushing the industry toward Sn-Ag-Cu (SAC) alloys instead. Aluminum-silicon casting alloys are the other classic case, eutectic at about 12.6 wt% Si and 577°C; because the eutectic composition has the lowest melting point and best fluidity in the whole system, near-eutectic Al-Si alloys are the workhorse of engine-block and automotive die casting. Aladar Pacz's 1921 discovery that adding a small amount of sodium refines the coarse, brittle plate-like silicon of an unmodified Al-Si eutectic into a fine fibrous form — dramatically improving ductility — remains the basis of modern Na- or Sr-modified casting alloys.

sections.heading: Lamellae, and what forms before the eutectic point
sections.body: At the eutectic composition itself, solidification produces a characteristic lamellar (alternating-layer) microstructure of alpha and beta plates growing side by side from the same solidification front, because that geometry lets each phase reject solute sideways into its neighbor over the shortest diffusion distance. Off-eutectic (hypo- or hyper-eutectic) compositions behave differently: cooling from the liquid, the alloy first passes through a single two-phase liquid-plus-alpha (or liquid-plus-beta) field above the eutectic temperature, so a primary (also called proeutectic) phase nucleates and grows as large grains before the remaining liquid — now driven to the eutectic composition — transforms via the eutectic reaction at 183°C or 577°C. The resulting microstructure is a mix of large primary grains embedded in a fine eutectic matrix, and the relative amount of each is exactly what the lever rule from the previous lesson predicts.

lessons.workedExample: A Pb-Sn alloy at 40 wt% Sn is cooled slowly from the melt. It is hypoeutectic (below the 61.9 wt% Sn eutectic composition), so it first enters a liquid-plus-alpha field, growing primary alpha (Pb-rich) grains as the liquid composition drifts along the liquidus toward 61.9% Sn. Once the liquid reaches exactly 61.9% Sn at 183°C, the remaining liquid transforms isothermally into the lamellar alpha-beta eutectic. Under a microscope this alloy shows large, roughly equiaxed primary alpha grains surrounded by a fine striped eutectic matrix — a fingerprint that immediately tells a trained viewer the alloy was hypoeutectic, not eutectic or hypereutectic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge looking at a cast or soldered sample will ask why the microstructure shows both large grains and a fine striped region, because that distinguishes a student who read the diagram from one who just melted metal and photographed it. A weak answer calls the whole structure 'the eutectic' without distinguishing primary grains from the eutectic matrix. A strong answer names the primary phase, explains it formed before the eutectic reaction while the composition was off-eutectic, and can estimate the primary-to-eutectic ratio using the lever rule applied just above the eutectic temperature.

questions.prompt: At the eutectic point of the Pb-Sn system, how many degrees of freedom does the phase rule allow?

explanations.a: F=2 would apply to a single-phase field, not a three-phase invariant point.
explanations.b: F=1 applies to an ordinary two-phase field like alpha-plus-liquid, not the eutectic point itself.
explanations.c: Correct — with C=2 and P=3 (liquid, alpha, beta all present), F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0, so the eutectic reaction occurs at one fixed temperature and composition, not a range.
explanations.d: F cannot exceed C=2 for this condensed system (reached at P=1); three phases coexisting gives F=2-3+1=0, not because of a C+1 ceiling.

questions.prompt: A hypoeutectic Pb-Sn alloy (below 61.9 wt% Sn) is cooled slowly from the liquid. What forms first, before the eutectic reaction occurs?

options.text: Lamellar alpha-beta eutectic directly
Primary (proeutectic) alpha grains
Primary (proeutectic) beta grains
Pure liquid tin

explanations.a: The lamellar eutectic only forms once the remaining liquid reaches exactly the eutectic composition at 183°C, which happens after primary solidification, not first.
explanations.b: Correct — a hypoeutectic (Sn-poor, Pb-rich side) composition enters the liquid-plus-alpha field first, so primary alpha (the Pb-rich solid solution) nucleates and grows before the eutectic reaction.
explanations.c: Beta (Sn-rich) would be the primary phase in a HYPEReutectic alloy, above 61.9 wt% Sn, not this hypoeutectic one.
explanations.d: Pure tin liquid does not selectively form; the liquid composition shifts continuously along the liquidus, it does not separate into a pure-element pocket.

questions.prompt: Match each system detail to its correct value.

right.text: 61.9 wt% Sn at 183°C
12.6 wt% Si at 577°C
Sodium modification refining plate-like Si into a fine fibrous form

questions.explanation: Pb-Sn's eutectic is 61.9 wt% Sn at 183°C; Al-Si's is about 12.6 wt% Si at 577°C; Pacz's 1921 sodium-modification discovery turned the coarse eutectic silicon into a fine, ductility-improving fibrous form.

questions.prompt: Order the microstructural events as a hypereutectic Al-Si alloy (above 12.6 wt% Si) cools from the melt to room temperature.

items.text: Fully liquid, above the liquidus
Primary beta (Si-rich) grains nucleate and grow as liquid composition shifts toward 12.6% Si
Remaining liquid reaches 12.6% Si and transforms isothermally at 577°C into lamellar alpha-beta eutectic
Room-temperature microstructure: primary Si grains in a fine eutectic matrix

questions.explanation: Cooling starts fully liquid, primary beta forms first on the Si-rich (hypereutectic) side as the liquid is driven toward the eutectic composition, the eutectic reaction converts the remaining liquid isothermally, and the final structure retains both the primary grains and the eutectic matrix.

lessons.label: Eutectoid, Peritectic & Intermetallic Compounds

sections.heading: Eutectoid: one solid splits into two
sections.body: A eutectoid reaction has the same isothermal, invariant character as a eutectic (F=0 by the phase rule) but starts from a solid instead of a liquid: one solid phase transforms into two different solids on cooling, written gamma → alpha + beta. The name itself signals the relationship — 'eutectoid' means 'eutectic-like.' The Fe-C system's eutectoid point sits at 0.76 wt% C and 727°C, where austenite (gamma, an FCC solid solution) decomposes into ferrite (alpha, BCC, only about 0.022 wt% C) and cementite (Fe3C, 6.67 wt% C), forming the lamellar microstructure called pearlite — a solid-state parallel to the liquid-to-lamellar eutectic seen in Pb-Sn. Because both parent and products are solid, eutectoid transformations rely entirely on solid-state diffusion, which is far slower than diffusion in a liquid, so eutectoid microstructures are unusually sensitive to cooling rate — the basis of the whole field of steel heat treatment covered in later units.

sections.heading: Peritectic: liquid plus solid make a new solid
sections.body: A peritectic reaction runs the opposite direction from a eutectic in terms of phase count on each side: liquid plus one solid combine, on cooling, into a single different solid — L + alpha → beta, again isothermal and invariant. The Fe-C system also has a peritectic, at 1493°C, where liquid (0.53 wt% C) reacts with delta-ferrite (0.09 wt% C) to form austenite (0.17 wt% C). Peritectics are mechanistically trickier than eutectics because the new solid phase (beta) forms as a shell around the existing alpha grains, at the interface between alpha and liquid; that shell can slow or block further diffusion between the two reactants, so peritectic reactions routinely fail to go to completion under real cooling rates, leaving untransformed alpha cores behind — a non-equilibrium effect distinct from, but related to, the coring covered in the next lesson.

sections.heading: Line compounds slice the diagram in two
sections.body: An intermetallic compound with a fixed, essentially non-negotiable stoichiometry — such as Mg2Si, at 36.6 wt% Si — appears on a phase diagram as a single vertical line rather than a field with any width, because it can accommodate almost no deviation in composition without becoming a different phase or a two-phase mixture. Mg2Si melts congruently (directly to a liquid of the same composition) at about 1085°C. That vertical line effectively cuts the full Mg-Si diagram into two independent sub-diagrams — Mg to Mg2Si, and Mg2Si to Si — each behaving like its own simple eutectic system with its own eutectic point. Not every compound is a stable, congruently melting one: Fe3C (cementite), the 6.67 wt% C compound central to steel, is thermodynamically metastable — the true equilibrium phase at that composition and temperature range is graphite, and given enough time or high enough temperature (as in gray cast iron) Fe3C will decompose into iron and graphite instead. Engineers still treat Fe-Fe3C as the working diagram for most steels because the decomposition into graphite is extremely sluggish under normal processing conditions.

lessons.workedExample: In the Fe-C system, an alloy is held exactly at the eutectoid composition, 0.76 wt% C, and slow-cooled through 727°C. By the phase rule, F=0 at that point, so the transformation happens at a fixed temperature: austenite decomposes entirely into alternating lamellae of ferrite (0.022 wt% C) and cementite (6.67 wt% C) — pearlite. Contrast this with the peritectic at 1493°C: liquid at 0.53 wt% C and delta-ferrite at 0.09 wt% C react to form austenite at 0.17 wt% C, but because the new austenite forms as a shell around the delta grains, real (non-infinitely-slow) cooling often leaves a delta-ferrite core encased in austenite rather than fully consuming it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots a vertical line or an unfamiliar three-phase point on a poster diagram will ask 'what reaction is that, and which side is liquid?' because eutectoid and peritectic reactions are easy to visually confuse with a eutectic if a student has only memorized 'invariant point = eutectic.' A weak answer calls every invariant point a eutectic. A strong answer checks which phases sit on which side of the reaction (solid-to-two-solids for eutectoid, liquid-plus-solid-to-one-solid for peritectic) and can name a real system, showing they read the diagram's phase labels rather than pattern-matching on shape alone.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a eutectoid reaction from a eutectic reaction?

options.text: A eutectoid starts from one solid and produces two solids; a eutectic starts from liquid and produces two solids
A eutectoid occurs at higher temperature than any eutectic
A eutectoid has F=1, a eutectic has F=0
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable

explanations.a: Correct — eutectoid: gamma(solid) → alpha + beta (two solids); eutectic: L(liquid) → alpha + beta (two solids). The parent phase is solid in one case and liquid in the other.
explanations.b: Temperature is not what defines the distinction; the Fe-C eutectoid (727°C) happens to be well below the Fe-C peritectic (1493°C), but that is system-specific, not a rule.
explanations.c: Both eutectoid and eutectic points are three-phase invariant reactions with F = C - P + 1 = 0; they do not differ in degrees of freedom.
explanations.d: The parent phase differs (solid versus liquid), which is a real physical distinction with real consequences for diffusion speed and microstructure.

questions.prompt: Why do peritectic reactions frequently fail to go to completion under normal (non-infinitely-slow) cooling?

options.text: Because peritectics only occur in systems with no solid solubility
Because the new solid phase forms as a shell around the existing solid, blocking further diffusion between reactants
Because peritectic temperatures are always below room temperature
Because liquid cannot coexist with solid at a peritectic point

explanations.a: Peritectic systems can and do have solid solubility ranges around the reaction, as in Fe-C where both delta and austenite are solid solutions.
explanations.b: Correct — the product phase nucleates at the alpha/liquid interface and grows as an encasing shell, so further reaction requires diffusion through that shell, which is slow and often incomplete under real cooling rates.
explanations.c: Peritectic temperatures are set by the specific system; Fe-C's peritectic is at 1493°C, far above room temperature.
explanations.d: A peritectic point is defined precisely by liquid and solid coexisting with a third solid phase, all at once, at F=0.

questions.prompt: Match each compound or reaction to its defining fact.

right.text: Congruently melting line compound at 36.6 wt% Si, about 1085°C
Metastable compound at 6.67 wt% C; true equilibrium favors graphite instead
0.76 wt% C, 727°C, austenite decomposes into ferrite plus cementite (pearlite)

questions.explanation: Mg2Si is a stable, congruently melting line compound; Fe3C is metastable relative to iron plus graphite; the Fe-C eutectoid at 0.76 wt% C and 727°C produces the ferrite-cementite lamellar structure called pearlite.

questions.prompt: Order these phases by carbon content, from lowest to highest wt% C, using the Fe-C values given in this lesson.

items.text: Ferrite (alpha) at the eutectoid, 0.022 wt% C
Delta-ferrite at the peritectic, 0.09 wt% C
Austenite at the peritectic, 0.17 wt% C
Eutectoid composition, 0.76 wt% C
Cementite (Fe3C), 6.67 wt% C

questions.explanation: Reading the carbon contents given in this lesson in increasing order: ferrite 0.022, delta-ferrite 0.09, austenite (peritectic) 0.17, the eutectoid composition 0.76, and cementite 6.67 wt% C.

lessons.label: Non-Equilibrium Cooling & Mapping to Microstructure

sections.heading: Why real cooling breaks the equilibrium picture
sections.body: Every tie line and lever-rule calculation so far assumed each phase has time to homogenize by solid-state diffusion at every temperature — an assumption that holds only in the limit of infinitely slow cooling. Solid-state diffusion is orders of magnitude slower than liquid diffusion, so as cooling rate increases, the solid phase stops keeping up: the composition at the center of a growing solid grain (set early, when the liquid was far from equilibrium) never fully re-equilibrates with the composition set later, near the grain's outer edge. The result is coring — a smooth composition gradient inside a single grain, richer in the higher-melting element at the core and richer in the lower-melting element toward the boundary, even though the equilibrium diagram predicts one uniform composition.

sections.heading: The Scheil equation quantifies the extreme case
sections.body: Erich Scheil formalized the opposite limiting case in 1942: assume zero diffusion in the solid (each shell of solid, once formed, is frozen in composition) but complete, instantaneous mixing in the liquid. Under those assumptions the Scheil equation predicts that solidification never actually completes at the equilibrium solidus — instead, a small amount of increasingly solute-enriched liquid persists to much lower temperatures than the equilibrium diagram shows, and the average solid composition trails behind the equilibrium solidus rather than tracking it. Real alloys fall between the two extremes (full equilibrium and Scheil's zero solid-diffusion limit), but the Scheil model is close enough to many real castings that it is the standard tool for predicting segregation severity and the practical freezing range of an alloy. Coring is corrected industrially by a homogenization anneal — holding the solid well below the solidus for hours, giving solid-state diffusion enough time to erase the composition gradient the equilibrium diagram assumed was never there.

sections.heading: Mapping a diagram point to what a microscope shows
sections.body: The payoff of this whole unit is the ability to go from any (composition, temperature) point to a prediction of what a polished, etched sample would show under a microscope: single-phase field → one uniform grain structure; two-phase liquid-plus-solid field on cooling → primary grains of the solid phase in a matrix that will become the other phase or a eutectic; eutectic composition → uniform fine lamellae with no primary phase; off-eutectic → primary grains plus eutectic matrix, in a ratio the lever rule predicts. But every one of those predictions is an equilibrium prediction, and this lesson's central limit is that no real microstructure is guaranteed to match it exactly — cored grains, retained non-equilibrium phases, and incomplete peritectic shells are the norm, not the exception. That gap between the clean equilibrium map and the messier real microstructure is exactly what motivates moving next to the iron-carbon system, where the metastable Fe-Fe3C diagram used throughout steel metallurgy is itself a deliberate, practically useful departure from true equilibrium.

lessons.workedExample: A Cu-Ni alloy at 35 wt% Ni is cast in a sand mold (moderate cooling rate, far from equilibrium) rather than furnace-cooled over days. Instead of a uniform 35 wt% Ni grain, a polished cross-section under a microscope shows cored dendrites: nickel-rich cores (formed early, near the solidus composition at the start of freezing) surrounded by progressively more copper-rich shells (formed later, as the liquid was enriched in copper). An electron microprobe line scan across one grain would show Ni content declining smoothly from center to edge — direct physical evidence of coring that a furnace-cooled control sample, given a homogenization anneal, would not show.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge examining an actual cast or etched sample will ask why the microstructure does not match the clean, single-composition prediction from the equilibrium phase diagram, because that question separates a student who treated the diagram as decoration from one who understands it as a limiting case. A weak answer insists the sample 'should' be uniform and has no explanation for what the microscope actually shows. A strong answer names coring, explains it comes from insufficient solid-state diffusion time relative to the real cooling rate, and can describe (or cite) the homogenization anneal as the practical fix.

questions.prompt: What assumption does the Scheil equation (Scheil, 1942) make about diffusion during solidification?

options.text: Complete diffusion in both the solid and the liquid
Zero diffusion in the solid, complete instantaneous mixing in the liquid
Zero diffusion in both the solid and the liquid
Complete diffusion in the solid, zero mixing in the liquid

explanations.a: Complete diffusion in both phases is the standard equilibrium assumption the phase diagram itself uses, not the Scheil model.
explanations.b: Correct — Scheil's 1942 model freezes each shell of solid at the composition it forms with (no further solid diffusion) while assuming the liquid stays perfectly mixed, the opposite extreme from full equilibrium.
explanations.c: Zero diffusion in the liquid would prevent any composition averaging and does not match the Scheil assumption of complete liquid mixing.
explanations.d: This inverts the actual assumption — Scheil assumes the SOLID is frozen and the LIQUID is well-mixed, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: What physically causes coring in a cast dendrite?

options.text: The mold cools the outside of the casting faster than the inside
Solid-state diffusion is too slow to keep the whole grain at the equilibrium composition as the liquid composition keeps changing during freezing
The alloy's overall composition changes during pouring
Coring only occurs in eutectic alloys, not isomorphous ones

explanations.a: Mold-driven thermal gradients affect grain size and orientation, but coring is a compositional gradient WITHIN a grain, caused by diffusion limits, not by which surface cools fastest.
