explanations.b: Correct — because solid-state diffusion cannot keep pace with the shifting liquid and solidus compositions during real (non-infinitely-slow) cooling, early-formed solid retains a different composition than later-formed solid within the same grain.
explanations.c: The overall alloy composition is fixed once poured; coring is a redistribution within that fixed total, not a change to it.
explanations.d: Coring is a general non-equilibrium solidification effect and appears in isomorphous systems like Cu-Ni just as readily as in others — this lesson's worked example is exactly a Cu-Ni case.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in fixing coring in a cast Cu-Ni part.

items.text: Alloy solidifies under real (fast, non-equilibrium) cooling, forming cored dendrites
Microprobe line scan across a grain shows Ni content declining from center to edge
Part is held at a homogenization temperature well below the solidus for an extended time
Solid-state diffusion evens out the gradient, leaving a uniform composition matching the equilibrium prediction

questions.explanation: Coring first forms during fast real-world solidification, is then identified by compositional mapping across a grain, is corrected by a long, sub-solidus homogenization anneal, and only after that anneal does the grain approach the uniform composition the equilibrium diagram originally predicted.

questions.prompt: Match each diagram region to the microstructure it predicts under equilibrium cooling.

left.text: Off-eutectic composition, cooled through liquid-plus-solid then the eutectic reaction

right.text: One uniform grain structure, no second phase
Primary grains of one phase embedded in a fine eutectic matrix
Uniform fine lamellae throughout, with no primary phase

questions.explanation: A single-phase field gives one uniform structure; an off-eutectic alloy forms primary grains before the eutectic reaction consumes the remaining liquid, leaving primary grains in a eutectic matrix; the exact eutectic composition forms only the lamellar eutectic structure, with no primary phase at all.

lessons.label: The Iron-Carbon (Fe-Fe3C) Diagram

sections.heading: Iron's Allotropy: Three Structures Before Carbon Even Joins In
sections.body: Pure iron does not have one crystal structure — it has three, each stable in its own temperature window, and this shape-shifting is what makes steel possible. Below 912°C, iron atoms pack into a body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice called alpha-ferrite. Heat past 912°C and the lattice reorganizes into face-centered cubic (FCC) austenite, gamma-iron, stable from 912°C to 1394°C. Push past 1394°C and iron flips back to a BCC arrangement, delta-ferrite, which persists until the metal melts at 1538°C. These are allotropic transitions, not melting or boiling — same element, different packing, because each structure minimizes free energy over a different temperature range. The FCC window matters enormously for practical metallurgy: FCC packing has larger, more symmetric octahedral interstitial sites than BCC, so austenite can dissolve far more carbon in solid solution than either ferrite form. Nearly every steel heat treatment — annealing, normalizing, quenching — starts by heating into the austenite field specifically to exploit that solubility.

sections.heading: Cementite and Why the Diagram Is Metastable
sections.body: Carbon does not dissolve indefinitely in iron; past its solubility limit it combines with iron to form cementite, Fe3C, an intermetallic compound fixed at 6.67 wt% carbon. Cementite is hard, brittle, and orthorhombic, and mixed with ferrite in varying proportions and geometries it produces essentially every steel microstructure in this unit. The diagram engineers actually use is the Fe-Fe3C diagram, and it is explicitly metastable: the true equilibrium product of carbon in iron, given enough time and temperature, is not cementite but graphite. Fe3C is thermodynamically metastable relative to Fe plus graphite, but decomposition is so sluggish under normal cooling rates that cementite persists indefinitely in steels. Only under very slow cooling combined with a graphitizing element like silicon — the situation in gray cast iron — does graphite form instead. Two iron-carbon alloys, otherwise similar, can behave very differently depending on which of these diagrams actually governs their cooling.

sections.heading: Reading the Diagram: The 2.14% Line and the Named Boundaries
sections.body: The vertical line at 2.14 wt% carbon, the maximum solubility of carbon in austenite, is the practical dividing line between steels (below, wrought and forgeable) and cast irons (above, brittle and cast to near-final shape). Metallurgists label key phase-boundary lines with letters: A3 marks the ferrite-to-austenite boundary on the carbon-lean side, Acm marks the austenite-to-cementite solubility boundary on the carbon-rich side, and A1 marks the eutectoid line at 727°C, which lessons 3 and 4 build on directly. Two invariant reactions anchor the diagram's geometry: a eutectoid point at 727°C and 0.76 wt% C, and, over on the cast-iron side, a eutectic point at 1147°C and 4.30 wt% C, where liquid solidifies directly into austenite plus cementite. The load-bearing fact for this unit: everything downstream — pearlite, bainite, martensite — is what austenite becomes on cooling, so locating where austenite exists is the prerequisite for all of it.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a 1040 steel, 0.40 wt% C, being prepared for normalizing. Follow the vertical line at 0.40% C upward on the Fe-Fe3C diagram: it crosses the A3 boundary around 810°C. Below that temperature the alloy is a two-phase mix of ferrite and austenite; above it, the alloy is single-phase austenite, homogeneous FCC iron with all 0.40% carbon in solid solution. A shop normalizing 1040 steel heats to roughly 860-890°C, about 50°C above A3 for a safety margin, holds until the austenite is uniform, then air-cools. Every subsequent microstructure in this unit describes what that homogeneous austenite becomes on the way back down — which is why locating A3 for a given composition is the first step of any heat-treatment plan, not an afterthought.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks why a student heated to that specific temperature before quenching is testing whether the diagram is a lookup table or an understood tool. A weak answer says 'the recipe said 850°C.' A strong answer explains the goal was single-phase austenite — enough above A3 to fully dissolve the carbon and homogenize the structure, but not so far above that austenite grains coarsen and later transformation products end up correspondingly coarse and weak. Naming A3 or Acm and tying the target temperature to the actual composition, rather than a generic 'red hot,' is the signal that separates a memorized shop procedure from applied understanding of the phase diagram.

questions.prompt: Why does FCC austenite dissolve far more carbon than BCC ferrite?

options.text: Austenite is a liquid phase, so carbon simply floats in it
Austenite's octahedral interstitial sites are larger and more symmetric than ferrite's, despite FCC being more densely packed overall
Carbon bonds covalently only in FCC iron
Ferrite has no interstitial sites at all

explanations.a: Austenite (gamma-iron) is solid, stable from 912-1394°C; it is not a liquid phase.
explanations.b: Correct — FCC's octahedral interstices are larger and more symmetric, so despite FCC's higher packing factor, austenite accommodates far more dissolved carbon (up to 2.14 wt%) than BCC ferrite (up to 0.022 wt%).
explanations.c: Carbon dissolves interstitially in both phases; there is no covalent-only mechanism unique to FCC iron.
explanations.d: BCC ferrite has interstitial sites too, just smaller and more distorted ones, which is why it still dissolves a small amount of carbon.

questions.prompt: Order iron's phases from lowest to highest stable temperature range.

items.text: Alpha-ferrite (BCC)
Austenite / gamma-iron (FCC)
Delta-ferrite (BCC)
Liquid iron

questions.explanation: Alpha-ferrite is stable up to 912°C, austenite from 912-1394°C, delta-ferrite from 1394°C up to the 1538°C melting point, above which iron is liquid.

questions.prompt: Match each phase to its crystal structure.

right.text: BCC
FCC
Orthorhombic

questions.explanation: Alpha- and delta-ferrite are both BCC (different temperature windows); austenite is FCC; cementite (Fe3C) is an orthorhombic intermetallic compound.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the Fe-Fe3C diagram is 'metastable'?

options.text: Cementite is the true equilibrium phase, so the diagram is fully accurate
The diagram only applies above 1000°C
Cementite is thermodynamically metastable relative to iron plus graphite, but decomposes so slowly under normal cooling that it persists indefinitely in steels
The diagram is wrong and metallurgists no longer use it

explanations.a: The true equilibrium product is graphite, not cementite; cementite only appears stable because decomposition is kinetically very slow.
explanations.b: The diagram covers the full temperature range from room temperature to melting, not just high temperatures.
explanations.c: Correct — Fe3C is metastable relative to Fe + graphite, but that decomposition is so sluggish under ordinary cooling rates that engineers treat the Fe-Fe3C diagram as accurate for steels.
explanations.d: The Fe-Fe3C diagram remains the standard working diagram for steel heat treatment; it is not obsolete.

lessons.label: Ferrite, Austenite & Cementite: The Building-Block Phases

sections.heading: Solubility Limits: What Each Phase Can Actually Hold
sections.body: Alpha-ferrite, BCC iron, dissolves at most 0.022 wt% carbon, and only at 727°C — cool it to room temperature and the solubility falls to roughly 0.005-0.008 wt%, essentially none. Austenite, FCC iron, dissolves up to 2.14 wt% carbon at 1147°C, nearly a hundred times more. The reason is geometric, not just thermal: FCC iron packs more densely overall (packing factor 0.74 versus BCC's 0.68), yet its octahedral interstitial sites are larger and more symmetric than the distorted sites available in the BCC lattice. A carbon atom, at roughly 0.077 nm radius, barely fits even the more accommodating FCC site and badly strains the tighter BCC one. So the phase that is more densely packed overall is, counterintuitively, the better solvent for carbon — packing factor and interstitial-site size are not the same property, and mixing them up is a common shortcut that gives the wrong intuition.

sections.heading: Mechanical Character: Soft Ferrite, Hard Brittle Cementite
sections.body: Alpha-ferrite is soft and ductile, with hardness around 80-100 HB and tensile strength near 150-200 MPa for essentially pure iron — comparable to mild aluminum, and it is the room-temperature ferromagnetic phase everyone pictures when they think 'iron.' Cementite, Fe3C, sits at the opposite extreme: hardness in the range of 800-1100 HV (roughly 68 HRC-equivalent) with essentially zero ductility, fracturing rather than deforming. It is only weakly ferromagnetic, and loses even that above its Curie temperature of about 210°C, well below its melting point. Because these two phases are the raw ingredients of nearly every steel microstructure, virtually every strengthening strategy in steel metallurgy — pearlite spacing, bainite morphology, martensite tempering — reduces to a question of how much cementite is present and how it is distributed relative to the soft ferrite matrix around it.

sections.heading: Austenite: The High-Temperature Workhorse
sections.body: Austenite itself is nonmagnetic (paramagnetic) and, because FCC crystals slip on genuinely close-packed {111} planes with low, largely temperature-independent lattice friction (Peierls-Nabarro) stress, it deforms easily and uniformly across a wide temperature range — unlike BCC ferrite, whose slip planes are only quasi-close-packed and carry a much higher lattice friction stress that drops enough for easy glide only at elevated temperature, which is exactly why hot-working operations like forging and hot rolling are done in the austenite range. But austenite is not a room-temperature phase in ordinary carbon steel; on cooling it must transform into something else, and what it transforms into — pearlite, bainite, or martensite — is the subject of the rest of this unit. Every one of those products is, at bottom, a different way of redistributing the same carbon that austenite held in solution between new ferrite and new cementite.

lessons.workedExample: A metallurgist runs a Vickers microhardness traverse across a polished, etched pearlite colony at 100x, planting indents roughly every 5 micrometers. The trace does not read as one number: it oscillates sharply between about 150 HV when the indenter lands on a ferrite lamella and 850-1000+ HV when it lands on a cementite lamella, even though both lamellae sit within the same microstructure a few micrometers apart. The bulk hardness reported for the pearlite colony as a whole — typically 200-300 HB — is essentially a weighted average of these two wildly different constituent hardnesses, which is the mechanical logic behind every composite steel microstructure in this unit.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the ferrite/cementite hardness contrast because it tests whether a student understands steel as a two-phase composite rather than a single material with one hardness number. A weak answer states 'steel is hard' without saying why. A strong answer names the two constituent phases, gives roughly correct hardness values for each, and explains that the OVERALL property of any microstructure in this unit — pearlite, bainite, even tempered martensite — is a mixture rule between soft ferrite and hard cementite, so controlling the amount and geometry of cementite is the entire lever available for tuning steel strength.

questions.prompt: Alpha-ferrite has a lower overall packing factor than austenite (0.68 vs 0.74), yet it dissolves far less carbon. Why?

options.text: Because ferrite's octahedral interstitial sites are smaller and more distorted than austenite's, even though ferrite has more open space overall
Because ferrite is a liquid phase at low temperature
Because carbon repels BCC iron atoms electrostatically
Packing factor and carbon solubility are unrelated coincidences with no explanation

explanations.a: Correct — overall packing factor is not the same as interstitial-site geometry; BCC's individual octahedral sites are smaller and more distorted, so they accept far less carbon despite the lattice having more open volume overall.
explanations.b: Alpha-ferrite is solid at all temperatures where it exists; it is never a liquid phase.
explanations.c: Carbon dissolves interstitially via a geometric size-and-strain effect, not an electrostatic repulsion mechanism.
explanations.d: There is a specific geometric reason (interstitial site size and distortion), not an unexplained coincidence.

questions.prompt: Order these phases by maximum carbon solubility, from lowest to highest.

items.text: Alpha-ferrite (max ~0.022 wt% C)
Austenite (max 2.14 wt% C)
Cementite (fixed at 6.67 wt% C)

questions.explanation: Alpha-ferrite tops out at 0.022 wt% C at 727°C, austenite reaches 2.14 wt% C at 1147°C, and cementite is a stoichiometric compound fixed at 6.67 wt% C — it does not have a solubility range at all.

questions.prompt: Match each phase to its defining mechanical/magnetic trait.

right.text: Soft, ductile, ferromagnetic at room temperature
Nonmagnetic, good high-temperature ductility, basis of hot working
Very hard, essentially zero ductility, loses magnetism above ~210°C

questions.explanation: Ferrite is the soft, ferromagnetic room-temperature phase; austenite is the nonmagnetic, formable high-temperature phase used for hot working; cementite is hard and brittle and only weakly ferromagnetic below its ~210°C Curie temperature.

lessons.label: The Eutectoid Reaction & Pearlite

sections.heading: The Eutectoid Point: One Solid Splitting Into Two
sections.body: A eutectoid reaction is a solid-state analogue of a eutectic: instead of a liquid splitting into two solids on cooling, one solid phase splits into two different solid phases at a single fixed temperature and composition. In the Fe-Fe3C system that point sits at 727°C and 0.76 wt% carbon, where austenite decomposes as it cools past that temperature into alpha-ferrite (0.022 wt% C) plus cementite (6.67 wt% C). Because the ferrite and cementite that form hold so much less and so much more carbon than the parent austenite, the reaction requires the carbon originally spread through the austenite to redistribute over short diffusion distances into the growing cementite plates while it is rejected from the growing ferrite plates. That diffusion requirement is the key fact this lesson turns on: unlike martensite (lesson 6), the eutectoid reaction is time- and temperature-dependent, not instantaneous.

sections.heading: Why Lamellae Form: The Pearlite Morphology
sections.body: The product of the eutectoid reaction is pearlite, alternating parallel plates (lamellae) of ferrite and cementite, named for the iridescent, mother-of-pearl-like sheen the fine lamellae give under an optical microscope as light diffracts off the layered structure. Pearlite nucleates at austenite grain boundaries and grows outward as roughly circular colonies, or nodules, within which all the lamellae share a common orientation. The lamellar geometry itself is a diffusion solution: carbon rejected from a growing ferrite plate does not have to travel far — just sideways to the neighboring cementite plate that is simultaneously absorbing it — so the two phases grow cooperatively, locked together, advancing into the untransformed austenite as a single coupled front.

sections.heading: Cooling Rate Sets Spacing, Spacing Sets Strength
sections.body: The eutectoid reaction is not a single number but a range: it can proceed anywhere from just below 727°C down to around 550°C before other transformation products (lesson 5) take over, and the transformation temperature within that range sets the interlamellar spacing. A slow furnace cool, transforming near 727°C where diffusion is fast and undercooling is small, produces coarse pearlite with spacing around 0.4-1 micrometer. Faster cooling — air cooling, transforming lower in the range — produces fine pearlite with spacing closer to 0.1-0.2 micrometer. Finer spacing means far more ferrite-cementite interface area per unit volume, and those interfaces impede dislocation motion, so fine pearlite is harder and stronger (roughly 300+ HB, tensile strength approaching 1000 MPa) than coarse pearlite (roughly 200 HB, around 700 MPa) of the identical composition — a reminder that spacing is a kinetic variable, not a compositional one.

lessons.workedExample: Two identical bars of 1080 steel (0.80 wt% C, essentially eutectoid) are austenitized at 850°C. One is furnace-cooled slowly through the 727°C eutectoid temperature; the other is removed and air-cooled. Both end up fully pearlitic, with the same 0.80% carbon content and the same ferrite-to-cementite ratio by the lever rule — but the furnace-cooled bar transformed close to 727°C and shows coarse lamellae under the microscope with Brinell hardness near 200 HB, while the air-cooled bar transformed lower in the range, shows visibly finer lamellae, and reads near 300 HB. Same composition, same phases present, different strength — purely from cooling rate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why is your fine-pearlite sample harder than your coarse-pearlite sample if they're the same steel' is testing whether a student conflates composition with cooling history. A weak answer reaches for a different alloy or a measurement error. A strong answer states plainly that both samples have identical 0.76-0.80 wt% carbon and the same ferrite/cementite fraction, and that the hardness difference comes entirely from interlamellar spacing set by transformation temperature — naming the mechanism (more interface area blocking dislocations) rather than just asserting that faster cooling makes things harder.

questions.prompt: At what temperature and composition does the eutectoid reaction occur in the Fe-Fe3C system?

explanations.a: That is the eutectic point (liquid to austenite plus cementite), a different invariant reaction on the cast-iron side of the diagram.
explanations.b: Correct — the eutectoid reaction, austenite to ferrite plus cementite, occurs at 727°C and 0.76 wt% C.
explanations.c: 1538°C is the melting point of pure iron, with no carbon and no eutectoid reaction involved.
explanations.d: 912°C is the pure-iron alpha-to-gamma allotropic transition temperature (0 wt% C), not the eutectoid point.

questions.prompt: Order these eutectoid transformation conditions from producing the coarsest pearlite to the finest.

items.text: Isothermal hold just below 727°C
Slow furnace cooling
Air cooling

questions.explanation: Transforming closer to 727°C gives faster diffusion and less undercooling, producing coarser lamellae; transforming lower in the eutectoid range (as with faster air cooling) gives finer, more closely spaced lamellae.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: 727°C and 0.76 wt% C, where austenite splits into ferrite and cementite
Alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite grown as a coupled diffusion front
The distance between adjacent lamellae, set by transformation temperature, controlling strength

questions.explanation: The eutectoid point is the fixed temperature/composition where the reaction occurs; pearlite is the lamellar product; interlamellar spacing is the kinetic variable that governs pearlite's strength.

questions.prompt: Why does the eutectoid reaction require time, unlike the diffusionless martensite transformation covered later in this unit?

options.text: Because carbon must diffuse short distances to build up the 6.67 wt% C cementite and deplete down to the 0.022 wt% C ferrite from the parent austenite's 0.76 wt% C
Because iron atoms must be transported across the entire sample
Because pearlite only forms above the melting point
There is no time dependence; pearlite forms instantly like martensite

explanations.a: Correct — ferrite and cementite have very different carbon contents from the parent austenite, so carbon must diffuse locally to feed the growing cementite plates and vacate the growing ferrite plates, which takes measurable time.
explanations.b: The redistribution is of carbon over short (lamellar-spacing-scale) distances, not bulk iron transport across the sample.
explanations.c: Pearlite forms well below the melting point, during cooling through the eutectoid temperature range.
explanations.d: Pearlite formation is diffusion-controlled and time-dependent, in direct contrast to the diffusionless, near-instantaneous martensite transformation.

lessons.label: Hypoeutectoid & Hypereutectoid Steels

sections.heading: Proeutectoid Ferrite: The Grain-Boundary Precursor
sections.body: Most steels are not exactly 0.76 wt% carbon, so most steels do not cool straight into 100% pearlite. In a hypoeutectoid steel (below 0.76 wt% C), cooling austenite first crosses the A3 line, and alpha-ferrite begins nucleating at the austenite grain boundaries well before the alloy reaches 727°C. This early-forming ferrite is called proeutectoid ferrite — 'pro' because it forms before the eutectoid reaction proper. As it grows, it rejects nearly all of its carbon into the shrinking pool of remaining austenite, enriching that austenite toward 0.76 wt% C. By the time the temperature reaches 727°C, the leftover austenite has reached the eutectoid composition and transforms entirely to pearlite, leaving a final microstructure of light-etching proeutectoid ferrite grains sitting alongside darker pearlite colonies.

sections.heading: Proeutectoid Cementite: The Embrittling Network
sections.body: Hypereutectoid steels (0.76-2.14 wt% C) run the same logic in reverse. Cooling austenite now crosses the Acm line instead of A3, and proeutectoid cementite precipitates first, again at the prior austenite grain boundaries, before the remaining austenite reaches 0.76 wt% C and transforms to pearlite. The practical difference matters: because cementite is hard and brittle rather than soft, it tends to form thin, continuous or semi-continuous films along the grain boundaries rather than isolated grains, creating a brittle network that gives crack propagation an easy path straight through the microstructure. This is a genuine concern in high-carbon tool and bearing steels — 52100 bearing steel (about 1.0 wt% C) is a standard example — and it is why such steels are routinely given a spheroidizing anneal, a long, low-temperature hold that breaks the grain-boundary cementite film into discrete rounded carbide particles instead.

sections.heading: The Lever Rule: Quantifying the Mixture
sections.body: Because the final microstructure is just a two-phase mixture — proeutectoid phase plus pearlite — the lever rule lets a student compute exact fractions from the overall carbon content, C0. For a hypoeutectoid steel, the fraction of pearlite is (C0 - 0.022)/(0.76 - 0.022), with the remainder being proeutectoid ferrite. For a hypereutectoid steel, the fraction of pearlite is (6.67 - C0)/(6.67 - 0.76), with the remainder being proeutectoid cementite. This is a straight application of the tie-line-and-lever construction any solid-solution phase diagram supports, just applied at the eutectoid line rather than at a two-liquid-phase boundary, and it runs both directions: given a composition, predict the micrograph; given an area-fraction estimate from a micrograph, back-calculate the carbon content.

lessons.workedExample: A 1040 steel, 0.40 wt% C, is slow-cooled from the austenite field. Applying the lever rule: fraction pearlite = (0.40 - 0.022)/(0.76 - 0.022) = 0.378/0.738 ≈ 0.51, so about 51% pearlite and 49% proeutectoid ferrite by area. A micrograph showing roughly equal parts light-etching ferrite grains and darker pearlite colonies is consistent with exactly this composition — which is the same 1040 steel used as the worked example in lesson 1, now explained at the microstructure level rather than just the single-phase-austenite level.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges hand over an unlabeled micrograph and ask 'what's the carbon content?' precisely because it separates vocabulary from quantitative fluency. A weak answer names the two constituents (ferrite, pearlite) and stops. A strong answer estimates the area fraction of each constituent from the image, plugs it into the lever rule to back-calculate an approximate wt% C, and — if the sample is hypereutectoid — separately flags a continuous grain-boundary cementite network as a toughness liability that a spheroidizing anneal would address, connecting composition, microstructure, and mechanical consequence in one answer.

questions.prompt: In a 0.90 wt% C steel cooled slowly from the austenite field, what forms first, before pearlite?

options.text: Proeutectoid ferrite at the grain boundaries
Proeutectoid cementite at the grain boundaries
Martensite
Nothing forms first; the steel goes directly to 100% pearlite

explanations.a: Proeutectoid ferrite forms only in hypoeutectoid steels, below 0.76 wt% C; 0.90 wt% C is hypereutectoid.
explanations.b: Correct — at 0.90 wt% C, above the 0.76 wt% eutectoid composition, cooling austenite crosses the Acm line and proeutectoid cementite precipitates at grain boundaries before the remaining austenite reaches the eutectoid composition and forms pearlite.
explanations.c: Martensite requires rapid quenching well below the eutectoid temperature range; it does not form on slow cooling.
explanations.d: Only an exactly eutectoid steel (0.76 wt% C) transforms directly to 100% pearlite with no proeutectoid phase; 0.90 wt% C is off that exact point.

questions.prompt: Order the events in slow cooling of a hypoeutectoid (e.g. 0.40 wt% C) steel from the austenite field.

items.text: Single-phase austenite above A3
Proeutectoid ferrite nucleates at austenite grain boundaries
Remaining austenite enriches toward 0.76 wt% C
Remaining austenite transforms to pearlite at 727°C

questions.explanation: Cooling starts in single-phase austenite, crosses A3 where proeutectoid ferrite begins forming at grain boundaries and rejecting carbon, which enriches the shrinking austenite pool until it reaches 0.76 wt% C at 727°C and transforms to pearlite.

questions.prompt: Match each steel type to the proeutectoid phase it forms on slow cooling.

right.text: Proeutectoid ferrite
Proeutectoid cementite
No proeutectoid phase — 100% pearlite

questions.explanation: Hypoeutectoid steels form proeutectoid ferrite, hypereutectoid steels form proeutectoid cementite, and a steel at exactly the eutectoid composition transforms directly to 100% pearlite with nothing proeutectoid at all.

questions.prompt: Using the lever rule, roughly what fraction of a 1.20 wt% C steel's slow-cooled microstructure is proeutectoid cementite?

options.text: About 7%
About 51%
About 93%
0%, since hypereutectoid steels form no proeutectoid phase

explanations.a: Correct — fraction proeutectoid cementite = (1.20 - 0.76)/(6.67 - 0.76) = 0.44/5.91 ≈ 0.074, about 7%, with the remaining roughly 93% being pearlite.
explanations.b: 51% is the pearlite fraction that would result from a hypoeutectoid steel near 0.40 wt% C (lesson's worked example), not this hypereutectoid calculation.
explanations.c: 93% is the correct pearlite fraction for this alloy, but the question asks for the proeutectoid cementite fraction, which is the smaller remainder.
explanations.d: Hypereutectoid steels do form a proeutectoid phase — cementite — it is just a small fraction close to the eutectoid composition.

lessons.label: Bainite: The Intermediate Transformation Product

sections.heading: Discovery and the Temperature Window
sections.body: Bainite takes its name from Edgar Bain, who with Edmund Davenport at U.S. Steel in 1930 systematically studied what happens when austenite is quenched and held isothermally at a series of fixed temperatures rather than simply cooled continuously — work that led directly to the time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram this lesson depends on. Their experiments revealed a transformation product distinct from both pearlite above it and martensite below it, occupying a temperature band roughly 250-550°C for a eutectoid steel. On a TTT diagram this window sits in the 'bay' between the pearlite C-curve and the martensite start temperature, and it behaves like neither neighbor cleanly: it shares pearlite's need for some carbon diffusion, yet it also involves a shear-like, martensite-flavored displacement of the parent lattice, which is why bainite is often described as a hybrid transformation mechanism.

sections.heading: Two Morphologies: Upper vs Lower Bainite
sections.body: Bainite that forms in the upper part of its temperature range, roughly 400-550°C, is called upper bainite: feathery sheaves of parallel ferrite laths with cementite particles precipitated between the laths, where diffusion is fast enough for carbon to escape the growing ferrite entirely. Lower in the range, roughly 250-400°C, diffusion is more sluggish and lower bainite forms instead — finer, more acicular ferrite plates, but now with fine carbide particles precipitating within the ferrite laths themselves, typically at about 55-60 degrees to the lath axis, giving it a superficial resemblance to tempered martensite under the microscope. Both morphologies are still, chemically, mixtures of ferrite and cementite like pearlite — what differs is scale and carbide placement, not the phases present.

sections.heading: The Strength-Toughness Payoff and Why It Is Absent from the Equilibrium Diagram
sections.body: Bainite's fine ferrite plates and finely dispersed carbides give it a better combination of strength and toughness than pearlite at comparable hardness, which is why bainitic microstructures show up deliberately in rail steel, in some high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) grades, and as a component of modern TRIP-assisted sheet steels. But bainite is conspicuously absent from the Fe-Fe3C phase diagram in lesson 1 — and that absence is itself the concept this lesson is teaching. The Fe-Fe3C diagram is an equilibrium diagram with no time axis; it tells you what phases are stable, not how fast or by what path they form. Bainite is purely a kinetic product, defined entirely by an isothermal hold or a continuous cooling rate that lands in its temperature-time window, so it can only be read off a TTT or continuous-cooling-transformation (CCT) diagram, never off the equilibrium diagram alone.

lessons.workedExample: A eutectoid steel is austenitized, then rapidly transferred into a molten salt bath held isothermally at 350°C. Reading a TTT diagram for this steel, the pearlite transformation nose sits around 550°C at roughly one second, but at 350°C the C-curve has moved out to several seconds to minutes before transformation starts, and the product forming in that lower-temperature bay is lower bainite rather than pearlite. Holding the bar in the bath until the transformation finishes, then air-cooling, yields a fully bainitic microstructure with no additional quenching step needed — an isothermal treatment called austempering, used specifically because it reaches bainite's strength-toughness balance without the distortion and cracking risk of a full martensitic quench.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why isn't bainite on the phase diagram you showed me' specifically to catch students who have memorized microstructure names without understanding what kind of diagram produces each one. A weak answer shrugs or claims the diagram is incomplete. A strong answer states plainly that the Fe-Fe3C diagram is an equilibrium diagram with no time axis, while bainite is a kinetic product that only exists because of a specific isothermal hold or cooling rate — and can point to where bainite would appear instead, on a TTT or CCT diagram, naming the temperature window (roughly 250-550°C) and the discoverers (Bain and Davenport, 1930).

questions.prompt: Bainite forms in roughly what temperature range for a eutectoid steel, and who first identified it as a distinct isothermal transformation product?

options.text: 700-900°C; identified by early X-ray diffraction studies of austenite
250-550°C; identified by Bain and Davenport in 1930
Below 0°C; identified during modern cryogenic treatment research
Exactly at 727°C; identified as part of the original Fe-Fe3C diagram

explanations.a: 700-900°C is above the eutectoid temperature entirely, in the austenite or ferrite+austenite field, not the bainite range.
explanations.b: Correct — bainite occupies roughly 250-550°C for a eutectoid steel, and was identified as a distinct isothermal transformation product by Bain and Davenport at U.S. Steel in 1930.
explanations.c: Cryogenic treatment addresses retained austenite in martensitic steels, a different topic from bainite's isothermal transformation window.
explanations.d: 727°C is the equilibrium eutectoid temperature for pearlite formation, not the bainite range, and bainite is not part of the original equilibrium diagram at all.

questions.prompt: Order these transformation products by the temperature at which they typically form, from highest to lowest.

items.text: Pearlite
Upper bainite
Lower bainite
Martensite

questions.explanation: Pearlite forms just below 727°C down to about 550°C, upper bainite forms roughly 400-550°C, lower bainite roughly 250-400°C, and martensite forms below the martensite start temperature, generally below bainite's range.

questions.prompt: Match each bainite morphology to where its carbide particles form relative to the ferrite laths.

right.text: Carbides precipitate between the ferrite laths
Carbides precipitate within the ferrite laths, at roughly 55-60 degrees to the lath axis

questions.explanation: Upper bainite forms at higher temperature where carbon can diffuse fully out of the ferrite laths, so carbides form between laths; lower bainite forms at lower temperature where diffusion is slower, so fine carbides precipitate inside the laths themselves.

questions.prompt: Why can bainite not be located on the equilibrium Fe-Fe3C phase diagram from lesson 1?

options.text: Because bainite has a different chemical composition than ferrite and cementite
Because the equilibrium diagram has no time axis, and bainite is a purely kinetic product defined by cooling rate or isothermal hold time
Because bainite only forms above the melting point of iron
Because the diagram was drawn before bainite was discovered and has never been updated

explanations.a: Bainite is chemically still ferrite plus cementite, the same phases as pearlite; the distinction is morphology and formation mechanism, not composition.
explanations.b: Correct — the Fe-Fe3C diagram shows equilibrium phases as a function of temperature and composition only; bainite's identity depends on the time-temperature path of cooling, which requires a TTT or CCT diagram to capture.
explanations.c: Bainite forms at 250-550°C, far below the melting point, not above it.
explanations.d: The diagram is not out of date; it is simply the wrong tool for a kinetic product, by design, regardless of when bainite was discovered.

lessons.label: Martensite: The Diffusionless Transformation

sections.heading: A Shear, Not a Diffusion
sections.body: Quench austenite fast enough — fast enough to outrun the pearlite and bainite noses on the TTT diagram entirely — and the carbon dissolved in it has nowhere to go. Instead of the diffusional redistribution that builds pearlite or bainite, the FCC austenite lattice shears cooperatively, atom by coordinated atom, into a new structure at a speed close to the speed of sound in the metal: essentially instantaneous, with no compositional change at all. The crystallographic path connecting the two lattices was worked out by Edgar Bain in 1924, now called the Bain strain, and the resulting structure is body-centered tetragonal (BCT) rather than the simple BCC of ordinary ferrite: the carbon atoms that would need to diffuse out to reach ferrite's low solubility limit instead stay trapped in interstitial sites, and that trapped carbon forces one lattice axis to stretch, distorting a cube into a slightly elongated tetragon.

sections.heading: Hardness Climbs Steeply With Carbon Content
sections.body: Because the tetragonal distortion and its associated lattice strain scale with how much carbon is trapped, martensite's hardness rises sharply with carbon content. Very-low-carbon martensite is only modestly hard, around 200 HV, while martensite at 0.6-0.8 wt% carbon reaches roughly 800-830 HV, on the order of 65 HRC — dramatically harder than any pearlite or bainite of the same composition, because the strengthening mechanism here is solid-solution and strain hardening from trapped carbon rather than a two-phase interface effect. Above about 0.6-0.8 wt% carbon the hardness gain levels off and can even dip slightly, because the martensite start and finish temperatures drop with rising carbon content, and above roughly 0.6 wt% C the finish temperature falls below room temperature — leaving soft, untransformed retained austenite trapped between the martensite plates, which pulls the bulk hardness back down even as the martensite itself keeps getting harder.

sections.heading: Lath vs Plate Morphology and As-Quenched Brittleness
sections.body: Below roughly 0.6 wt% carbon, martensite forms as lath martensite: packets of fine, parallel laths bundled into blocks, relatively tougher than the alternative. Above roughly 1.0 wt% carbon, it forms instead as plate (lenticular) martensite: coarser individual lens-shaped plates, often with a visible midrib, more brittle, and frequently separated by thin films of the retained austenite just described. Either way, as-quenched martensite is hard, brittle, and carries substantial internal residual stress, driven both by thermal gradients from the rapid quench and by the roughly 2-4% volume expansion that accompanies the shear transformation itself. That combination of hardness, brittleness, and stress is precisely why as-quenched martensite is essentially never used in service — it is virtually always tempered afterward, reheated to relieve stress and precipitate some of the trapped carbon as fine carbides, trading a slice of hardness for the toughness the as-quenched state lacks.

lessons.workedExample: Two bars are austenitized and water-quenched. A 1020 steel bar (0.20 wt% C) forms lath martensite throughout its cross-section fairly easily, reaching a modest hardness around 40 HRC, and stays reasonably tough because low-carbon lath martensite has fewer of the internal carbide films that promote cracking. A 1095 steel bar (0.95 wt% C), quenched into brine for a faster cooling rate, forms plate martensite mixed with visible retained austenite, reaching a much higher hardness near 65 HRC — but it is now so brittle and internally stressed that it must be tempered within hours of quenching, before residual stress alone can crack the part, a well-known shop hazard with high-carbon tool steels.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why doesn't martensite show up as a sloped line on the equilibrium phase diagram the way pearlite formation does' is testing whether a student actually understands diffusionless transformation, not just the word. A weak answer conflates martensite with just 'fast pearlite.' A strong answer states that martensite formation is athermal and essentially time-independent below the martensite start temperature — it depends on how far below Ms the sample is, not on how long it is held there — in direct contrast to the diffusion-and-time-controlled formation of pearlite and bainite, and can connect that distinction to why martensite requires a TTT or CCT diagram's Ms/Mf lines rather than a C-curve.

questions.prompt: What crystal structure does martensite have, and why?

options.text: FCC, because it retains austenite's original structure unchanged
Body-centered tetragonal (BCT), because carbon trapped in solution by the diffusionless shear distorts the BCC lattice along one axis
Orthorhombic, the same structure as cementite
Simple cubic, unique among all iron-carbon phases

explanations.a: Martensite forms from austenite via a shear transformation but is not FCC itself; the shear converts the lattice to a distorted BCC-derived structure.
explanations.b: Correct — the diffusionless shear transformation follows the Bain strain path from FCC to a BCC-derived lattice, and carbon trapped interstitially (rather than diffusing out) elongates one axis, producing body-centered tetragonal martensite.
explanations.c: Cementite's orthorhombic structure is a separate, stoichiometric intermetallic compound, unrelated to martensite's BCT structure.
explanations.d: Martensite is body-centered tetragonal, not simple cubic; no phase in this unit has a simple cubic structure.

questions.prompt: Order these steels' as-quenched martensite by increasing hardness.

items.text: Very low carbon (~0.05 wt% C)
Medium carbon (~0.4 wt% C)
Eutectoid range (~0.7 wt% C)

questions.explanation: Martensite hardness rises steeply with carbon content because more trapped interstitial carbon produces more lattice strain, so hardness increases from very low carbon up through the eutectoid range before the gain levels off near 0.6-0.8 wt% C.

questions.prompt: Match each carbon range to the martensite morphology it typically produces.

right.text: Lath martensite: fine parallel laths in packets, relatively tougher
Plate (lenticular) martensite: coarser individual plates with a midrib, more brittle, often with retained austenite films

questions.explanation: Low-to-medium-carbon steels form fine lath martensite; high-carbon steels form coarser, more brittle plate martensite, frequently with retained austenite trapped between plates because the martensite finish temperature drops below room temperature at high carbon content.

questions.prompt: Why is as-quenched martensite almost never used directly in service without further processing?

options.text: It is too soft to be useful until strengthened further
It is hard, brittle, and carries high internal residual stress from the rapid quench and the transformation's volume expansion, so it is virtually always tempered afterward
It spontaneously reverts back to austenite within minutes at room temperature
It has no practical hardness advantage over pearlite

explanations.a: As-quenched martensite is typically the hardest microstructure available for a given composition, not too soft — the problem is brittleness and stress, not lack of hardness.
explanations.b: Correct — the combination of high hardness, low ductility, and residual stress from thermal gradients and the transformation's roughly 2-4% volume expansion makes as-quenched martensite crack-prone, so tempering is standard practice.
explanations.c: Martensite is a stable-enough room-temperature structure that it does not spontaneously revert to austenite on its own; tempering is a deliberate reheating step, not a spontaneous reversal.
explanations.d: Martensite is substantially harder than pearlite at the same carbon content, which is exactly why it is used at all despite needing tempering afterward.

lessons.label: Reading Steel Microstructures

sections.heading: A Field Guide Under the Microscope
sections.body: After a standard nital etch, the five microstructures from this unit each have a recognizable signature at moderate optical magnification. Proeutectoid ferrite appears as light-etching, roughly equiaxed polygonal grains. Pearlite shows the alternating light-and-dark banding of its ferrite-cementite lamellae, or, at lower magnification, a coarse 'fingerprint' texture where individual lamellae blur together. Bainite etches darker and more uniformly than pearlite, appearing feathery (upper bainite) or finely acicular (lower bainite), with its lamellae generally too fine to resolve clearly even at high magnification, in contrast to pearlite's cleanly visible plates. Martensite appears as sharply defined needle-like or lens-shaped plates, heavily etched dark, often arranged in packets; untempered martensite in particular can show a fine 'rice grain' texture. Cementite itself, whether proeutectoid or lamellar, tends to stand out as bright, lightly etched regions or networks against the darker ferrite-rich background.

sections.heading: Mapping Composition and Cooling History onto Structure
sections.body: The single hardest habit for a student to build is remembering that composition and cooling path answer two different questions. The exact same 0.76 wt% carbon (eutectoid) steel can end up as coarse pearlite, fine pearlite, bainite, or martensite depending entirely on how it was cooled — composition, via the Fe-Fe3C diagram and the lever rule from lessons 1 and 4, sets what phases and phase fractions are even possible at equilibrium, while the cooling path, read off a TTT or CCT diagram as covered in lessons 5 and 6, determines which of those kinetically available products actually forms. Reading an unlabeled micrograph correctly means using both diagrams together: composition narrows the field of what is chemically consistent, and morphology (lamellar versus feathery versus acicular versus needle-like) picks out which one actually happened.

sections.heading: A Decision Tree
sections.body: A working procedure for an unlabeled sample: first, estimate wt% carbon from any visible proeutectoid phase and its lever-rule fraction, which places the steel as hypoeutectoid, eutectoid, or hypereutectoid. Second, read the transformation product's morphology to infer the cooling path — coarse lamellae point to a slow furnace cool near 727°C; fine lamellae point to a faster, still-diffusional cool; feathery or acicular non-lamellar structure points to an isothermal hold or continuous cool through the 250-550°C bainite bay; needle-like plates with very high hardness point to a fast quench below the martensite start temperature. Cross-checking that inferred cooling path against an independent hardness measurement is the final step — a sample that looks feathery under the microscope but reads 65 HRC is inconsistent with bainite alone and should prompt a second look for a mixed or misread structure.

lessons.workedExample: A student is handed an unlabeled micrograph showing dark, needle-like plates with no resolvable lamellae, arranged in overlapping packets, plus a reported hardness of 60 HRC. Working the decision tree: the morphology (fine acicular plates, no lamellae) and the hardness (far above the ~300 HB ceiling of even fine pearlite or bainite) both point to martensite, meaning the sample was quenched fast enough to bypass the pearlite and bainite noses entirely. If thin white films are also visible threading between the plates, that additionally suggests retained austenite, which points toward a carbon content above roughly 0.6 wt% C, since above that level the martensite finish temperature drops below room temperature.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges hand over exactly this pairing — an unlabeled micrograph plus a hardness number — because it forces the two-diagram synthesis this whole unit builds toward. A weak answer names one microstructure from appearance alone and stops. A strong answer states the morphology, states the hardness, checks that the two are mutually consistent (a feathery structure with martensite-range hardness is a red flag, not a confirmation), and states what specific cooling path — isothermal hold, quench, furnace cool — would be needed to produce that combination, tying it back to a named diagram (Fe-Fe3C for composition, TTT or CCT for the path) rather than to memorized appearance alone.

questions.prompt: Match each microscope appearance to the microstructure it indicates.

left.text: Alternating light/dark lamellae, resolvable at high magnification
Feathery or finely acicular, darker, lamellae not clearly resolvable
Sharp needle-like or lens-shaped plates, heavily etched dark, very high hardness

right.text: Proeutectoid ferrite
Pearlite
Bainite
Martensite

questions.explanation: Ferrite grains are light and equiaxed; pearlite shows resolvable lamellae; bainite is darker and feathery/acicular with lamellae too fine to resolve clearly; martensite is sharply needle-like or lenticular with very high hardness.

questions.prompt: Order these microstructures from lowest to highest typical hardness, for a given carbon content.

items.text: Proeutectoid ferrite
Pearlite
Bainite
Martensite

questions.explanation: Soft, single-phase ferrite is lowest; pearlite's coarser ferrite-cementite lamellae are next; bainite's finer ferrite-carbide structure is generally harder than pearlite; as-quenched martensite, with its trapped-carbon lattice strain, is highest.

questions.prompt: A eutectoid (0.76 wt% C) steel can end up as coarse pearlite, fine pearlite, bainite, or martensite. What determines which one actually forms?

options.text: The carbon content, since each product requires a different wt% C
The cooling path (cooling rate or isothermal hold temperature), read from a TTT or CCT diagram, not the Fe-Fe3C equilibrium diagram alone
The grain size of the original casting
Nothing; the product is random for a fixed composition

explanations.a: All four products can occur at the same 0.76 wt% C; composition alone does not distinguish among them, since it is fixed here.
explanations.b: Correct — with composition fixed at the eutectoid point, it is specifically the time-temperature cooling path that selects which product forms, which is why a TTT or CCT diagram, not the equilibrium diagram, is the tool for predicting it.
explanations.c: Original grain size can influence nucleation site density and thus fineness within a given product, but it does not determine which of the four product types forms.
explanations.d: The outcome is fully determined by the cooling path, not random; a TTT/CCT diagram predicts it precisely for a given time-temperature history.

lessons.label: Annealing: Full, Process & Spheroidizing

sections.heading: Full annealing: austenitize, then cool as slowly as the furnace allows
sections.body: Full annealing softens steel to its most workable state by heating it fully into the austenite field and cooling it slowly enough that transformation happens near equilibrium. For hypoeutectoid steel that means 30-50 C above the A3 line; for hypereutectoid steel (above about 0.8% C) the target is only 30-50 C above A1, not above Acm. Heating a hypereutectoid steel above Acm dissolves all the cementite, and slow furnace cooling from there reprecipitates it as a continuous, brittle network along the austenite grain boundaries - exactly the microstructure a machinist does not want. Staying just above A1 keeps some spheroidal cementite undissolved, so the proeutectoid phase never gets the chance to form that grain-boundary film. After soaking, the furnace is shut off or ramped down at roughly 10-20 C per hour, letting austenite decompose into coarse pearlite: thick alternating ferrite/cementite lamellae that are soft, low-strength, and easy to machine.

sections.heading: Process and stress-relief annealing: softening without crossing A1
sections.body: Not every anneal re-austenitizes the steel. Process annealing (also called subcritical or intermediate annealing) heats cold-worked low-carbon steel to 550-650 C, below A1, purely to recrystallize the strained, elongated ferrite grains left by wire drawing or deep drawing. Because no phase change occurs, it is cheap and fast, and shops use it between drawing passes to restore ductility before the next reduction. Stress-relief annealing sits at a similar or slightly lower range (roughly 500-650 C) and is not about softening the matrix at all - it is aimed at residual stresses locked in by welding, machining, or casting, which it relieves through localized creep and recovery without materially changing hardness or grain size.

sections.heading: Spheroidizing: chasing the cementite into spheres
sections.body: Spheroidizing pushes ductility further than any other anneal by converting cementite - whether lamellar pearlite or a grain-boundary network - into discrete spheroids dispersed through a ferrite matrix (spheroidite). The driving force is the same one that drives Ostwald ripening anywhere: a sphere has the least interfacial area per unit volume, so the system lowers its interfacial energy by pinching lamellae into balls given enough time near A1, typically 650-700 C for many hours, sometimes with thermal cycling just above and below A1 to accelerate the process. High-carbon tool and bearing steels are spheroidized before cold heading or thread rolling, because spheroidite's low strength and high ductility let it flow rather than crack under the punch.

lessons.workedExample: A shop receives 1080 steel (0.8% C, essentially eutectoid) bar stock straight from hot rolling, coarse pearlite already present, and needs to cold-head it into fastener blanks. Cold heading that bar as-received would crack the lamellar pearlite. Instead they spheroidize: hold at 700 C, just under A1, for 12-15 hours, letting the pearlite's cementite lamellae ball up into spheroidite. The resulting structure - soft ferrite riddled with rounded carbide particles - can absorb the severe local strain of heading without fracturing. After forming, the parts are austenitized and quenched to regain the hardness the spheroidizing anneal deliberately gave away.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you choose that specific anneal' because full, process, stress-relief, and spheroidize annealing solve different problems and a student who says 'we annealed it to make it softer' hasn't shown they know which one. A strong answer names the target microstructure (coarse pearlite vs. recrystallized ferrite vs. spheroidite) and ties it to what the part needs next - machining, cold forming, or just stress relief after welding. A weak answer treats every anneal as interchangeable heat-then-cool-slowly, which misses that process and stress-relief anneals never cross A1 at all.

questions.prompt: Why is a hypereutectoid steel full-annealed by heating just above A1 rather than above Acm?

options.text: Heating above Acm is too expensive in furnace time
Above Acm, slow cooling reprecipitates cementite as a brittle grain-boundary network
Acm cannot be reached in a standard furnace
Above Acm the steel decarburizes instantly

explanations.a: Cost isn't the driver; the microstructural outcome is.
explanations.b: Correct - dissolving all cementite above Acm lets it reform as a continuous grain-boundary film on slow cooling, which is brittle and undesirable.
explanations.c: Acm is well within normal furnace range for these steels.
explanations.d: Decarburization is an atmosphere-control issue, not the reason for this temperature choice.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes process annealing from full annealing?

options.text: Process annealing uses a faster furnace cool
Process annealing stays below A1, so no austenite forms
Process annealing is only for cast iron
Process annealing produces coarse pearlite

explanations.a: Cooling rate isn't the defining difference; both can be slow.
explanations.b: Correct - process annealing recrystallizes cold-worked ferrite entirely below A1, with no phase transformation.
explanations.c: Process annealing is a common step for cold-worked steel, not cast iron.
explanations.d: Coarse pearlite requires austenitizing above A1/A3 first, which process annealing does not do.

questions.prompt: Match each anneal type to its primary purpose.

right.text: Maximize machinability/softness via coarse pearlite from full austenitizing
Recrystallize cold-worked ferrite between drawing passes, no phase change
Convert cementite into spheroids for maximum ductility before cold forming

questions.explanation: Full annealing re-austenitizes and slow-cools for coarse pearlite; process annealing recrystallizes ferrite subcritically; spheroidizing coalesces cementite into spheroids for the softest, most formable structure.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as a shop would spheroidize eutectoid bar stock destined for cold heading.

items.text: Receive bar stock with as-rolled coarse pearlite
Hold near 700 C, just under A1, for many hours
Cementite lamellae coalesce into spheroidite
Cold-head the softened blanks without cracking

questions.explanation: The bar starts with lamellar pearlite, the long subcritical soak drives cementite to spheroidize by lowering interfacial energy, and only the resulting soft spheroidite can survive severe cold-heading strain.

questions.prompt: Why does cementite coalesce into spheres rather than staying as lamellae during a long spheroidizing hold?

options.text: Spheres have less interfacial area per unit volume, lowering interfacial energy
Magnetic domains realign cementite into spheres
Spheres are the only shape stable below A1
Furnace convection currents physically roll the lamellae into balls

explanations.a: Correct - this is Ostwald-ripening-style behavior: the system reduces total interfacial energy by minimizing surface area per volume, which a sphere does best.
explanations.b: Magnetism is unrelated to this diffusion-driven morphology change.
explanations.c: Lamellar cementite is metastable, not unstable, below A1; it just takes long diffusion times to spheroidize.
explanations.d: The process is diffusional, not mechanical.

lessons.label: Normalizing vs. Annealing

sections.heading: Same austenitizing step, a very different cool
sections.body: Normalizing starts the same way full annealing does - heating hypoeutectoid steel above A3 or hypereutectoid steel above Acm - but normalizing heats 30-60 C above A3 (vs. full annealing's 30-50 C above A3 for hypoeutectoid steel) and then removes the part from the furnace entirely, letting it air cool on a rack instead of cooling with the furnace. That single change in cooling environment matters enormously. A furnace cools at perhaps 10-20 C per hour; still air cools a small part orders of magnitude faster, often on the order of hundreds of degrees per minute for the first stretch. Faster cooling through the pearlite range means less time for carbon to diffuse over long distances, so the pearlite that forms has a finer interlamellar spacing - thinner, more closely packed ferrite and cementite plates. Finer pearlite is stronger and harder than the coarse pearlite from full annealing, by the same Hall-Petch-style logic that finer microstructures resist dislocation motion better: more phase boundaries to block slip.

sections.heading: Why the higher austenitizing temperature is not incidental
sections.body: Normalizing's 30-60 C of superheat above A3/Acm is deliberate, not just a rounding difference from annealing practice. Coarse-grained austenite - the kind left behind by casting, hot rolling at high temperature, or forging - carries that coarse grain size straight through into the room-temperature product if the steel is only reheated to the minimum annealing temperature. Overshooting further above A3/Acm gives full re-austenitization with enough thermal energy to nucleate a fresh, fine set of austenite grains throughout the section, refining what was there before. That refined grain size is normalizing's second selling point beyond the finer pearlite itself, and it is why normalizing is a standard prior step before final hardening: it erases the memory of prior thermal history (banding, coarse cast dendrites, forging-induced grain growth) so the subsequent quench starts from a uniform, fine-grained baseline instead of an inherited, inconsistent one.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
sections.body: A designer reaches for full annealing when the part needs maximum softness and machinability and cost of cycle time is secondary - annealing cycles run long because the furnace itself must cool slowly. Normalizing is chosen when moderate strength and toughness with less distortion risk than a full hardening quench are acceptable, when a uniform fine grain structure is needed before a later hardening operation, or simply when cycle time matters, since air cooling is far faster than furnace cooling. Structural steel shapes, forgings, and castings destined for as-normalized service commonly stop here rather than proceeding to a full quench-and-temper cycle.

lessons.workedExample: A forging shop produces medium-carbon steel gear blanks. As-forged, the blanks have coarse, non-uniform austenite grains from sitting at forging temperature, and if hardened directly they would show inconsistent case depth and poor toughness. The shop normalizes first: reheat to about 50 C above A3, hold briefly, then air cool on racks. This refines the grain size uniformly across the blank and leaves fine pearlite with decent strength as an intermediate condition. Only after normalizing do they proceed to austenitize again and oil-quench for final hardening - the normalizing step guarantees every blank starts the hardening cycle from the same fine-grained baseline instead of whatever grain size each forging happened to retain.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes normalizing vs. annealing to see whether a student understands that cooling rate, not just peak temperature, controls the final microstructure. A strong answer explains that air cooling gives less time for carbon diffusion than furnace cooling, producing finer pearlite and higher strength, and separately names grain refinement of a coarse cast/forged structure as normalizing's other job. A weak answer just says 'normalizing is annealing but faster' without connecting cooling rate to lamellar spacing or explaining why the higher austenitizing temperature is deliberately chosen.

questions.prompt: Why does normalizing produce finer pearlite than full annealing?

options.text: Normalizing uses a lower austenitizing temperature
Air cooling is faster than furnace cooling, giving less time for carbon to diffuse into thick lamellae
Normalizing forms bainite instead of pearlite
Normalizing is done in a vacuum, changing the diffusion mechanism

explanations.a: Normalizing actually uses a higher austenitizing temperature than full annealing.
explanations.b: Correct - faster cooling limits the distance carbon can diffuse, producing thinner, more closely spaced ferrite/cementite lamellae.
explanations.c: Plain-carbon normalizing typically still produces pearlite, just finer; bainite requires faster cooling than still air usually provides in bulk sections.
explanations.d: Normalizing is done in ordinary air, not a vacuum; atmosphere isn't the reason for the finer structure.

questions.prompt: Why does normalizing use an austenitizing temperature 30-60 C above A3/Acm, a wider margin than full annealing's 30-50 C above A3?

options.text: To fully melt any retained cementite network
To ensure full re-austenitization and refine a coarse prior grain structure
Higher temperature is needed to reach A1 in alloy steels
It has no real effect; it is just traditional practice

explanations.a: Melting isn't relevant at these solid-state heat-treatment temperatures.
explanations.b: Correct - the extra superheat guarantees complete austenitizing and nucleates a fresh, finer grain structure that erases coarse grains inherited from casting or forging.
explanations.c: A1 is a fixed transformation temperature for a given composition, not something that requires extra superheat to reach.
explanations.d: The extra temperature has a specific grain-refinement purpose, not mere tradition.

questions.prompt: Match each treatment to its typical cooling method.

right.text: Furnace cool (slow, ~10-20 C/hr)
Still air cool (much faster than furnace)

questions.explanation: Full annealing cools with the furnace for near-equilibrium, coarse pearlite; normalizing removes the part to air, cooling much faster for finer pearlite.

questions.prompt: Order a forging shop's process from as-forged blank to a normalized, fine-grained part ready for hardening.

items.text: As-forged blank has coarse, non-uniform austenite grains
Reheat 30-60 C above A3 to fully re-austenitize
Remove from furnace and air cool
Uniform fine-grained structure with fine pearlite results

questions.explanation: Normalizing starts from a coarse-grained forged part, re-austenitizes fully at elevated temperature to reset grain size, then air cools to lock in fine pearlite and refined grains.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a structural steel forging to have moderate strength, minimal distortion risk, and short cycle time, without needing maximum softness for machining. Which treatment fits best?

options.text: Full annealing
Normalizing
Spheroidizing
Stress-relief annealing only

explanations.a: Full annealing maximizes softness at the cost of long furnace cool cycles, more than needed here.
explanations.b: Correct - normalizing gives moderate-to-good strength from fine pearlite, refines grain structure, and finishes in a fraction of annealing's cycle time via air cooling.
explanations.c: Spheroidizing targets maximum ductility for cold forming, not general structural strength.
explanations.d: Stress relief alone does not address grain refinement or provide the strength increase normalizing gives.

lessons.label: Isothermal Transformation: TTT Diagrams

sections.heading: Reading a C-curve
sections.body: A time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram plots, for a steel held at a series of fixed temperatures below A1 after being quenched there instantly from austenite, how long it takes for austenite decomposition to start and finish at each temperature. For eutectoid steel (about 0.8% C) the result, first mapped systematically by Davenport and Bain (1930) at U.S. Steel, is a pair of C-shaped curves: one marking transformation start, one marking transformation finish, both bulging leftward toward short times at an intermediate temperature and stretching rightward toward long times as the hold temperature approaches either A1 or the martensite start temperature. The diagram only applies to an isothermal hold - the sample is assumed to drop to the hold temperature essentially instantly and then sit there, which is a lab idealization, not what a real quench does, but it is the cleanest way to isolate transformation kinetics from cooling-rate effects.

sections.heading: Why the curve has a nose at all
sections.body: The C-curve's leftmost point - the nose, at roughly 550 C for eutectoid steel with a start time of about one second - exists because austenite decomposition depends on two competing factors that move in opposite directions as temperature drops. Near A1, the thermodynamic driving force (the free-energy difference between austenite and the ferrite-plus-cementite product) is small, since the two phases are nearly in equilibrium there, so nucleation is slow even though atoms diffuse quickly at that temperature. Far below A1, the driving force is large, but diffusion of carbon - which must partition between carbon-poor ferrite and carbon-rich cementite - becomes sluggish as temperature falls. Overall transformation rate is fastest where the product of driving force and diffusivity peaks, at an intermediate temperature, and that peak rate is the nose. This driving-force-versus-diffusivity tradeoff is the same competition that governs nucleation kinetics generally, formalized later in Avrami-type transformation-rate equations.

sections.heading: Two different products above and below the nose
sections.body: Holding above the nose (between about 550 C and A1) gives pearlite, with lamellar spacing getting finer as the hold temperature drops toward the nose - coarse pearlite near A1, fine pearlite just above 550 C. Holding below the nose (between about 550 C and the martensite start temperature) gives bainite instead: upper bainite, feathery and forming around 400-550 C, transitioning to lower bainite, acicular and harder, below about 400 C. Both pearlite and bainite are diffusional, nucleation-and-growth products that need time at temperature to complete; only quenching straight past the nose down below the martensite start temperature bypasses diffusion entirely and produces martensite instead.

lessons.workedExample: A student holds a small eutectoid-steel sample isothermally at 600 C after austenitizing, per the TTT diagram, and finds the transformation-start curve crosses that temperature line around 5 seconds and the finish curve around 30 seconds. Between roughly 5 and 30 seconds, austenite is progressively converting to pearlite; holding to 30 seconds and beyond yields fully pearlitic microstructure appropriate for that temperature - coarser than a hold nearer the 550 C nose would give, because 600 C sits closer to A1 where lamellar spacing is wider. If the student instead held at 300 C, the same diagram would show a start time far to the right of the nose but the product would be lower bainite, not pearlite, because 300 C lies below the nose temperature.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about TTT diagrams because reading a start/finish curve correctly - and explaining why the curve has the C-shape it does - separates a student who memorized 'the nose is where it transforms fastest' from one who understands the driving-force/diffusivity tradeoff behind it. A strong answer connects hold temperature to which product forms (pearlite above the nose, bainite below it) and explains the nose mechanistically. A weak answer can point at the nose on a diagram but cannot say why it sits at an intermediate temperature rather than right next to A1.

questions.prompt: Why does the C-curve's nose occur at an intermediate temperature rather than right at A1?

options.text: Diffusivity is highest at the nose temperature

Transformation rate is fastest where driving force and diffusivity are both reasonably large, which peaks at an intermediate temperature since driving force grows with undercooling while diffusivity shrinks
The nose marks where cementite melts
Below A1 all temperatures transform at the same rate

explanations.a: Diffusivity is actually highest near A1, not at the nose; the nose is a compromise, not a diffusivity maximum.
explanations.b: Correct - the nose is where the product of driving force (large well below A1) and diffusivity (large near A1) is maximized.
explanations.c: Cementite does not melt at these solid-state transformation temperatures.
explanations.d: Transformation rate varies strongly with temperature, which is exactly why the curve has a C-shape rather than a flat line.

questions.prompt: In the eutectoid TTT diagram described, roughly what temperature and start time mark the nose?

options.text: About 550 C, about one second
About 727 C, about one hour
About 200 C, about one minute
About 900 C, about one second

explanations.a: Correct - this matches the nose location described in the lesson for eutectoid steel.
explanations.b: 727 C is near A1, where transformation is slow, not the fast-transforming nose.
explanations.c: 200 C is near or below the martensite start range, not the pearlite/bainite nose.
explanations.d: 900 C is well into the austenite field, above A1, where no isothermal transformation curve applies.

questions.prompt: Match each isothermal hold temperature range to the transformation product it yields.

left.text: Just below A1, well above the nose
Between the nose and martensite start

right.text: Coarse pearlite
Fine pearlite
Bainite

questions.explanation: Pearlite forms above the nose, coarsening as the hold temperature rises toward A1 and refining as it approaches the nose; below the nose, diffusional transformation instead produces bainite.

questions.prompt: Order these isothermal hold temperatures for eutectoid steel from fastest transformation start time to slowest.

items.text: 550 C (the nose)
700 C (near A1)

questions.explanation: Transformation is fastest at the nose (550 C) and slows as the hold temperature rises toward A1, where driving force shrinks even though diffusion is quick.

questions.prompt: What assumption does a TTT diagram make that a real industrial quench usually violates?

options.text: That the steel is eutectoid composition
That the sample cools essentially instantly to the hold temperature and then stays there isothermally
That carbon does not diffuse at all
That martensite never forms

explanations.a: Composition is a real, stated property of the diagram, not a violated assumption - though TTT diagrams differ by composition, that isn't the idealization in question.
explanations.b: Correct - real parts cool continuously through a range of temperatures rather than dropping instantly to one hold temperature, which is why continuous-cooling behavior needs its own diagram.
explanations.c: Carbon diffusion is exactly what drives pearlite and bainite formation on a TTT diagram; it isn't assumed absent.
explanations.d: Martensite can and does form on TTT diagrams below the martensite start temperature.

lessons.label: Continuous Cooling: CCT Diagrams & Critical Cooling Rate

sections.heading: Why continuous cooling needs its own diagram
sections.body: A TTT diagram assumes the sample drops instantly to a fixed hold temperature - useful for isolating pure transformation kinetics, but not what happens in an actual quench, where the part cools continuously through a whole range of temperatures on its way down. A continuous-cooling-transformation (CCT) diagram plots the same start-and-finish idea but for cooling curves instead of isothermal holds, and its C-curves sit shifted down and to the right relative to the TTT diagram for the same steel. The shift happens because during continuous cooling the sample only spends a limited amount of time passing through any given temperature band on its way further down, so more total time (and often a somewhat lower effective temperature) is needed before enough of that band's transformation accumulates to register as 'started' or 'finished' - the moving target of a falling temperature delays the reaction relative to a steady isothermal hold at the same point.

sections.heading: The critical cooling rate and missing the nose
sections.body: Superimposed on a CCT diagram, an actual cooling curve is a line running from the austenitizing temperature down through time; where that line intersects the pearlite or bainite start curve tells you the product. The critical cooling rate is the slowest continuous cooling rate that manages to miss the nose of the CCT curve entirely, dropping the sample below the martensite start temperature before any pearlite or bainite has had time to nucleate. Cool any slower and the curve clips the nose, letting some diffusional product form before martensite finally takes over below Ms - producing a mixed microstructure with lower hardness than a fully martensitic part. For plain-carbon eutectoid steel this critical rate is severe, on the order of hundreds of degrees Celsius per second, which is why a genuinely full-martensite plain-carbon part usually needs a fast water or brine quench and still only hardens fully in thin sections; a thick section's interior simply cannot lose heat that fast no matter how aggressive the surface quench.

sections.heading: Superimposing real quench media
sections.body: Overlaying representative cooling curves for furnace cooling, still air, oil, and water onto the same CCT diagram turns it into a practical prediction tool. A furnace-cool curve is nearly vertical-then-flat on a log-time axis and crosses well to the right of the nose, landing in the coarse-pearlite region. An air-cool curve is steeper, crossing closer to (but usually still right of) the nose for plain-carbon steel, giving fine pearlite. Oil quenching is steeper still and, for many alloy steels, threads between the nose and the bainite region, producing a mixed fine-pearlite/bainite structure depending on exact composition and section size. Water quenching is the steepest common curve, and for thin sections of eutectoid steel it can clear the nose outright, yielding martensite; the same water quench on a thick section may still miss the interior, because the surface cools far faster than the core.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know why a 25 mm diameter plain-carbon eutectoid steel rod water-quenched from austenitizing temperature comes out fully martensitic at the surface but shows a mottled, softer core with visible pearlite under the microscope. Plotting the surface and center cooling curves on the steel's CCT diagram explains it directly: the surface curve, cooling at a rate far above the critical cooling rate, drops straight past the nose into the martensite field. The center, insulated by the rod's own mass, cools more slowly - its curve clips the nose of the pearlite start region before continuing down, so some pearlite forms there before the remaining austenite finally transforms to martensite below Ms, leaving the mixed structure the student observed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing CCT understanding wants to see the student connect an observed mixed or inconsistent microstructure to an actual cooling-rate argument rather than a vague 'it didn't cool fast enough.' A strong answer explains that the CCT nose sits below and to the right of the TTT nose because continuous cooling only passes through each temperature briefly, and can name the critical cooling rate as the threshold that clears the nose.
