lessons.workedExample: A surgeon needs an intervertebral spacer for spinal fusion. Titanium is strong but has an elastic modulus roughly 5-10x that of cortical bone, so it carries almost all the load and shields the surrounding bone from mechanical stress, which triggers bone resorption over time (stress shielding) and also blocks CT/MRI imaging of the fusion site. PEEK's modulus is much closer to bone's, sharing load more naturally, and it's radiolucent, letting surgeons see fusion progress on imaging - the reason PEEK became the standard engineering-plastic choice for this application despite costing far more than a commodity resin.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why this specific polymer and not a cheaper one?' to see whether material choice was reasoned from competing requirements or just picked because it was on hand. A weak answer says 'PEEK is strong.' A strong answer names the actual competing requirements at stake - modulus match to bone versus cost, or oxygen barrier versus moisture sensitivity in EVOH - and explains the specific property tradeoff the chosen material and construction (like a multilayer film) were built to solve.

questions.prompt: Why is PEEK often chosen over titanium for a spinal fusion cage despite costing far more?

options.text: PEEK's elastic modulus is much closer to bone's, reducing stress shielding, and it is radiolucent for imaging
PEEK is stronger in absolute terms than titanium
PEEK is a commodity plastic, so it is actually the cheaper option
PEEK biodegrades after the fusion heals, unlike titanium

explanations.a: Correct - titanium's much higher modulus causes stress shielding and bone resorption, and it blocks imaging, while PEEK's bone-like modulus and radiolucency avoid both problems.
explanations.b: Titanium has higher absolute strength and stiffness than PEEK; PEEK's advantage here is a closer property match to bone, not superior raw strength.
explanations.c: PEEK is an engineering plastic priced well above commodity resins, not a cheap commodity material.
explanations.d: PEEK spinal implants are not designed to resorb; that behavior describes PLGA-type resorbable devices, a different biomedical polymer covered in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each application to the polymer property that drives its selection.

right.text: EVOH's very low oxygen permeability, protected from moisture by outer PE/PP layers
PEEK's bone-like elastic modulus and radiolucency
PLGA's tunable hydrolytic degradation rate, set by the lactide-to-glycolide ratio

questions.explanation: Barrier packaging is driven by EVOH's oxygen-barrier performance (protected structurally from moisture); a fusion cage is driven by PEEK's mechanical and imaging compatibility with bone; a resorbable suture is driven by PLGA's controllable hydrolysis rate.

questions.prompt: Order the stages by which a PLGA resorbable suture disappears in the body.

items.text: Water penetrates the PLGA matrix and begins hydrolyzing ester linkages
Average molecular weight drops as backbone chains are cut
The matrix begins measurable mass loss/erosion as fragments become small enough to be cleared
The implant is fully resorbed

questions.explanation: Hydrolysis first cuts backbone bonds (lowering molecular weight) well before the matrix loses measurable mass, and only after significant fragmentation does the implant fully disappear - which is why degradation rate is engineered through the lactide:glycolide ratio rather than left to chance.

questions.prompt: Why is EVOH used as a thin inner layer in a multilayer bottle rather than as the entire bottle wall by itself?

options.text: EVOH's excellent oxygen barrier performance degrades badly when it absorbs moisture, so outer PE/PP layers keep water away from it
EVOH is too expensive to be used at all, even as a thin layer
EVOH cannot be extruded and must be applied as a coating after molding
EVOH provides no oxygen barrier benefit and is included only for stiffness

explanations.a: Correct - EVOH is moisture-sensitive; its hydrogen-bonded structure swells and loses barrier performance when wet, so it needs moisture-blocking layers around it to function.
explanations.b: It is used specifically because a thin layer is affordable while delivering an outsized barrier benefit; the issue is a performance limitation (moisture sensitivity), not pure cost.
explanations.c: EVOH is co-extruded together with the other layers in standard multilayer packaging processes.
explanations.d: EVOH is included specifically for its oxygen barrier performance, which is far better than PET's or PE's alone.
